articles.title: How AI Erodes People’s Sense of Value at Work
articles.takeaway: The title says AI can erode people's sense of value at work, and the abstract fragment says the piece turns to what leaders can do about it. Only the title and a final line are available, so the theory below is a framework for testing the claim against the full article, not a summary of its findings.
articles.summary: This is an HBR piece whose title states that AI erodes people's sense of value at work. The only other text supplied is a line indicating that the article moves on to what leaders can do about this. The full argument, evidence and recommendations are not in the material provided, so nothing beyond the title and that closing line should be attributed to the article.
keyPoints: The headline claim is that AI erodes people's sense of value at work, which is a question about meaning and worth rather than only about tasks or productivity.
The abstract signals that the article treats leaders' response as central, so leadership is part of the argument.
Only the title and one line of the abstract are available, so any finding, figure or example must be checked against the full text before it is used in an assignment.
Sense of value at work can be analysed through job characteristics, the psychological contract and engagement, which are all taught in Unit 3 of PWO.

modules.reading: In PWO terms this is about what happens to motivation and engagement when AI changes the content of jobs. Value at work is closely tied to whether people experience their tasks as meaningful, whether they have autonomy and whether their skills are used. A student should care because the article's concern maps onto job design, the psychological contract and engagement, all of which are examinable in Unit 3, and because the leaders' response it promises belongs to how organisations manage individual differences and change.

The abstract's closing line places leaders' response at the centre of the piece. From the leadership module's point of view, the question is which leadership style or behaviour can restore people's sense of worth when work is being reshaped by technology. A student should care because the module asks how leaders influence motivation and meaning, and this article offers a live case to test transformational and other leadership theories against.

applications.concept: Job Characteristics Model (Hackman and Oldham)
applications.theory: The Job Characteristics Model holds that five core job dimensions (skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback) shape three psychological states: experienced meaningfulness, responsibility for outcomes and knowledge of results. These states in turn drive internal motivation, satisfaction and performance, and the model is used to redesign jobs so that they score higher on the dimensions.
applications.link: The title's claim that AI erodes sense of value can be read through the model's psychological state of experienced meaningfulness, which depends on task significance and skill variety. If AI takes over the varied or judgement-based parts of a role, the remaining work may score lower on skill variety and task identity, and workers may feel their contribution matters less. The full article should be checked for whether it describes this mechanism, and the abstract's focus on leaders suggests it proposes ways to redesign roles rather than only documenting losses.
applications.critique: The model was built around manufacturing and clerical jobs and treats job characteristics as stable features of a role, whereas AI can change them quickly and unevenly across a team. It also relies on self-reported perceptions, so a fall in perceived value may reflect expectations and fairness as much as the design of the job.
applications.practice: A manager applying the model would audit each role against the five dimensions before and after an AI tool is introduced, looking for lost variety or autonomy. Where meaningfulness has fallen, they would redesign the remaining work, for example by giving people ownership of the outputs AI produces or of the client relationships it cannot handle, and would build in feedback on those outcomes.

applications.concept: Psychological contract (Rousseau)
applications.theory: The psychological contract is the set of unwritten beliefs about mutual obligations between an employee and an employer, such as expectations of development, job security and recognition in return for effort and loyalty. A breach occurs when one party is perceived to have failed to deliver what was promised, and this can reduce trust, commitment and engagement.
applications.link: Introducing AI can change what employees believe they were promised, for example that their expertise would be developed and rewarded or that their role would grow with the firm. If the article argues that people's sense of value is eroding, the psychological contract explains why this may be felt as a breach rather than as a simple change in tasks. The abstract's emphasis on leaders suggests the article sees renegotiating these expectations openly as part of the response.
applications.critique: The psychological contract is inferred from perceptions and is hard to observe or measure, and it is not a formal document that leaders can simply rewrite. Critics would also say that the framework places responsibility on the employer's communication, when some erosion of value may come from the technology itself rather than from broken promises.
applications.practice: A leader would make explicit what the organisation still promises under AI, such as reskilling, job security or a new role, and would test whether employees share that understanding. They would then keep the commitments made, since visible follow-through does most to protect trust in the contract.

applications.concept: Transformational leadership (Bass)
applications.theory: Bass extended Burns's work to describe transformational leadership, which raises followers' awareness of what matters and motivates them to act for the group's goals rather than their own. It works through four components: idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration. It is contrasted with transactional leadership, which relies on exchanges of rewards for performance.
applications.link: If AI is eroding people's sense of value, a transactional response of incentives and monitoring would not address the question of meaning that the title raises. Transformational leadership offers a more direct fit, since intellectual stimulation can help people see how their judgement and expertise remain central, and individualised consideration can address the particular losses each person faces. The abstract's focus on what leaders can do suggests the article is making a similar case, though the full text is needed to confirm the specific behaviours it recommends.
applications.critique: Transformational leadership has been criticised for its vague and idealised character, and its effects are often measured through followers' ratings of the leader, which may overstate impact. It also gives little guidance on what to do when the leader's own role and job security are uncertain under AI.
applications.practice: A leader would explain clearly how AI changes the purpose of the team's work and would invite people to shape how it is used, giving them a visible role in the change. They would also check in with individuals on what they find meaningful, and would adjust tasks and recognition to match.

caseStudy.scenario: A professional services firm introduces AI tools that now produce a large share of the first drafts its analysts used to write. Some staff report feeling that their expertise matters less, and turnover in one team has begun to rise. The senior leadership team must decide how to respond and what to tell its people.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate how the firm's leaders should respond to the erosion of their staff's sense of value at work, drawing on theories of motivation, job design and leadership.
evidence: The article's title states that AI erodes people's sense of value at work, which can be used as the central claim to test against theory.
The abstract indicates that the article addresses what leaders can do about this erosion, so the leaders' response is a stated concern of the piece.
Specific data, examples or findings from the full article should be added here after reading it, as the abstract supplied does not contain them.
plan: Define sense of value at work and explain why it matters for motivation and engagement, citing the title's claim as the starting point.
Apply the Job Characteristics Model to diagnose which of the five core dimensions AI has reduced in the analysts' roles, and link this to experienced meaningfulness.
Use the psychological contract to examine whether staff now perceive a breach of promises about development, security or recognition, and identify what must be clarified.
Apply transformational leadership, distinguishing it from transactional responses, to show how leaders can restore meaning through intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration.
Critically assess the limits of these theories, such as the focus on perception and the difficulty of measuring the contract, and weigh them against the costs of the options.
Recommend a specific set of actions for the leadership team, including job redesign, open communication about commitments and an agreed way to measure whether value is recovering.
pitfalls: Asserting the article's findings or examples without having read the full text, since only the title and a closing line are available.
Treating AI as a simple cause of lost value without considering how leaders' choices in redesigning work and communicating change affect the outcome.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether the introduction of AI erodes people's sense of value at work, and assess what leaders can do to protect it.
outline: Define sense of value at work and explain its links to motivation, meaning and engagement, using job design and the psychological contract.
Assess the evidence and mechanisms by which AI may change job characteristics and expectations, and identify the limits of the theories used.
Evaluate the leadership responses available, such as transformational leadership and job redesign, and recommend a justified course of action.

articles.title: Why Employees Choose Purpose Over Pay
articles.takeaway: A strong social mission may help a startup attract talented staff while spending less on pay, which makes it a live question about what motivates people to join and stay, and how the employment bargain is struck. Only the abstract was available, so the notes rely on the abstract's claims and on theory rather than on findings from the full research.
articles.summary: The publisher's abstract summarises a discussion by J. Daniel Kim, Wharton assistant professor of management, of new research. According to the abstract, a strong social mission can help startups recruit talented employees while also reducing labour costs. The full article, the study design, sample and figures were not provided, so nothing beyond this headline claim can be reported with confidence. The note therefore treats the claim as a starting point and uses the People, Work and Organisations theories on motivation, the psychological contract and person-organisation fit to show how the effect could work and where it might break down.
keyPoints: The research, as summarised, links a strong social mission to two outcomes for startups: easier recruitment of talented people and lower labour costs.
The mechanism implied by the abstract is that employees value purpose enough to accept less pay or fewer conventional rewards than they could get elsewhere.
Because the abstract is short, the evidence base (sample, method, size of the effect, time frame) is unknown and should not be assumed.

Two theories from People, Work and Organisations help explain the claim: intrinsic motivation from purpose (self-determination theory) and the exchange of promises between employer and employee (psychological contract).
Herzberg's two-factor theory offers a way to think about pay and purpose as different kinds of workplace factor, though its direct application to recruitment is a stretch.

modules.reading: In the language of People, Work and Organisations, the abstract describes employees choosing a mission over higher pay, which is a question about what motivates people and what they value in work. It touches on motivation and engagement, since purpose may act as a source of intrinsic motivation, and on individual differences, since people differ in how much they value meaning relative to income. It also raises the psychological contract, because a mission-led employer may offer non-financial promises in exchange for lower pay. A student should care because the finding challenges a simple pay-led view of recruitment and asks how the employment deal is understood by the person making it.

In the strategy module the abstract suggests a mission can be a source of advantage in the labour market, because it helps a startup attract talent and lower its cost base. This connects to the resource-based view and VRIO, where a resource gives advantage if it is valuable, rare, hard to imitate and organised to be exploited. The connection is secondary, since the abstract says nothing about competitive positioning or market outcomes. A student should care because it shows how a non-financial asset can have financial effects that appear in a business model.

applications.concept: Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan)
applications.theory: Self-determination theory holds that people are motivated most strongly when three psychological needs are met: autonomy, competence and relatedness. Intrinsic motivation grows when work satisfies these needs, and extrinsic rewards such as pay can weaken intrinsic motivation when they are seen as controlling rather than informational. Motivation therefore depends on the quality of the regulation of behaviour, not only on its size.
applications.link: The abstract says a strong social mission helps startups recruit talented people, which suggests that purpose is valued for its own sake and can stand in for a higher salary. Under self-determination theory, a mission gives work a sense of meaning and direction that can satisfy relatedness and a sense of contributing, so pay becomes less central to the decision. This would explain why employees might accept lower labour costs without seeing it as a loss. The abstract, however, does not report whether the employees in the research were motivated in this way or whether they simply valued the mission at entry.
applications.critique: Self-determination theory describes what sustains motivation once someone is in a role, and it does not directly explain why people choose one employer over another. A mission may be a sign of an employer that supports autonomy and competence, but it may also be used as a recruitment message without these conditions, in which case the motivation would not last.
applications.practice: A startup founder applying this theory should show new hires how their work serves the mission, but also build autonomy and development into roles so the mission is backed by real opportunities to grow. Managers should avoid tying the mission to rigid rules and monitoring, since these can undermine the intrinsic motivation that the mission is meant to create.

applications.concept: The psychological contract (Rousseau)
applications.theory: The psychological contract is the set of beliefs an individual holds about the mutual obligations between themselves and their employer, beyond what is written in the formal contract. Rousseau distinguishes transactional contracts, based on specific and short-term exchanges such as pay for effort, from relational contracts, based on loyalty, long-term commitment and shared purpose. Breach occurs when an employee perceives that the employer has failed to deliver promised obligations, and this can reduce trust and commitment.
applications.link: The abstract describes employees trading some pay for a social mission, which is a clear example of a relational element entering the deal. The mission can be understood as a promise the employer makes, and employees who accept lower pay are relying on that promise being kept. This fits the idea that the contract is partly psychological and partly based on shared beliefs about purpose. The abstract does not say how staff experienced the mission after joining, so whether the contract was honoured is unknown.
applications.critique: Rousseau's model stresses perceptions, so the contract is only as strong as the employee's belief in it, and employers may not know what staff have understood. A mission-based offer can create high expectations that are hard to meet in a fast-changing startup, which makes breach more likely and could produce disillusionment greater than with a plain pay deal.
applications.practice: A manager should make the mission concrete in recruitment conversations, stating what it will mean for work, workload and career paths, and then check regularly whether employees still believe the promise is being kept. Where the startup cannot deliver some promised elements, it should say so early to limit the damage from perceived breach.

applications.concept: Herzberg's two-factor theory
applications.theory: Herzberg's two-factor theory divides workplace factors into hygiene factors, such as pay, working conditions and supervision, and motivators, such as achievement, recognition, the work itself and responsibility. Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction when adequate but do not create satisfaction, whereas motivators produce satisfaction and effort. The theory implies that pay alone cannot be the main source of motivation.
applications.link: The abstract's claim that purpose can attract talent while reducing labour costs fits the idea that meaningful work is a motivator that can offset a lower hygiene factor. Under this reading, a strong mission would give employees satisfaction from the work itself, so they would not need the same pay to remain content. The abstract does not state what employees gave up, so the theory can only suggest a mechanism rather than confirm it.
applications.critique: The two-factor theory is based on a limited and self-reported sample, and its clean split between hygiene and motivators has been criticised in later research. Pay can act as a motivator for some people, and people with financial pressures may not accept lower pay regardless of purpose, so the theory may overstate how far pay can be traded for meaning.
applications.practice: A founder using this theory should use the mission to build motivators, such as responsibility, achievement and recognition for contributions to the mission, while making sure pay and conditions are fair enough to avoid dissatisfaction. The aim is to avoid sending the message that low pay is acceptable simply because the work is meaningful.

applications.concept: The resource-based view and VRIO (Barney)
applications.theory: The resource-based view argues that a firm's competitive advantage comes from resources it controls. VRIO asks whether a resource is valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organised to be exploited, and only resources meeting all four conditions are likely to give sustained advantage. Resources such as culture, reputation and employee commitment can meet these tests when they are embedded in the organisation.
applications.link: The abstract suggests a social mission helps a startup attract talented staff at lower cost, which is a value-creating outcome. A mission that is genuinely held and difficult to copy could be rare and inimitable, since rivals cannot simply buy it, and the startup would need to organise recruitment and management to exploit it. The abstract does not establish that the mission is rare or that competitors cannot copy it, so these conditions remain assumptions.
applications.critique: Missions are easy to announce, and many firms adopt similar language, which weakens rarity and imitability. The VRIO framework also treats resources as relatively static, while a startup's mission may depend heavily on its founders and may fade as the firm grows.
applications.practice: A startup leader applying VRIO should test whether the mission is actually distinctive and whether it is embedded in hiring, reward and decision-making, rather than only in public statements. If it passes these tests, the leader should protect it through governance, such as mission-linked criteria for hiring and promotion, so it stays organised for exploitation.

caseStudy.scenario: A young technology startup with a strong social mission is competing for scarce engineering and product talent against larger firms that pay more. It has limited cash and wants to keep its labour costs low while still hiring people who can build the business. The founders are considering how much to emphasise the mission in recruitment and how to reward early employees.
caseStudy.question: Advise the founders on how a strong social mission might help the startup recruit talented staff while controlling labour costs, and critically evaluate the risks of relying on mission to replace pay.
evidence: Research discussed by J. Daniel Kim of Wharton shows that a strong social mission can help startups recruit talented employees.
The same research indicates that a social mission can also reduce labour costs for startups.
The abstract is a summary only, so the size of the effect, the sample and the time period are not known and should be noted as limitations.
plan: Set out the claim: according to the research summary, mission helps recruit talent and lowers labour costs, and state that the full evidence was not reviewed.
Apply self-determination theory to explain why purpose can motivate people beyond pay, and identify the autonomy, competence and relatedness the startup must provide.
Apply the psychological contract to show that a mission is a relational promise, and discuss the risk of perceived breach if the mission is not reflected in day-to-day work.
Use Herzberg's two-factor theory to argue that mission can work as a motivator, but that pay must remain adequate to avoid dissatisfaction.
Use the resource-based view and VRIO to test whether the mission is a sustainable advantage, noting that it must be genuine, distinctive and embedded in management.
Recommend that the founders use the mission to attract people who share its values, back it with autonomy, development and fair pay, and monitor whether the psychological contract is being honoured.
pitfalls: Treating the abstract's finding as proven in general, when the source offers only a summary of new research and no detail on method or scale.
Assuming that employees simply accept lower pay, without considering that some may accept it only in the short term or that mission may be a weaker motivator for people with financial pressures.

alsoConsider: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation (Deci and Ryan)

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that employees will accept lower pay in exchange for a sense of purpose, and discuss the implications for organisations seeking to recruit and retain talented staff.
outline: Explain the theories that account for purpose-driven motivation, including self-determination theory and Herzberg's two-factor theory, and show how each treats pay differently.
Analyse the psychological contract and self-selection as mechanisms that could explain recruitment, and identify the risks of perceived breach when a mission is not delivered in practice.

Evaluate the limits of the claim, including the unknown size of the effect, the risk of mission rhetoric without substance, and the financial pressures that may stop some people from accepting lower pay, and conclude with recommendations for employers.

articles.title: Coach, don’t rescue: Why HR should stop solving every people problem
articles.takeaway: When HR routinely solves line managers' people problems, managers grow less capable, employees bypass them, and HR loses time for strategic work. HR should coach managers through everyday issues, reserve direct intervention for legal, safeguarding and serious risks, and judge its value by how few problems need escalating.
articles.summary: The article argues that HR is often the default route for difficult people issues such as avoided performance conversations, team tension and concerns raised too late. This leaves managers less capable, encourages employees to go round their line manager, and stretches HR between reactive casework and strategic work. The author argues that line managers shape the employee experience more than any policy, so HR should coach them by asking what has happened, what has been said, what they are worried about and what outcome they want, rather than drafting wording, joining meetings or taking over. HR should still step in for legal, safeguarding, serious employee relations and significant organisational risk. Manager development should be continuous and built on real situations, managers need clear boundaries on when to act and when to escalate, and HR should measure success by whether problems are handled earlier and at the right level. The piece is practitioner opinion; it cites the CIPD's view on line manager capability but presents no original data.
keyPoints: HR is often the first port of call for difficult people issues, which can make managers less capable and HR less strategic.
Line managers have a larger influence on employee experience than any policy or HR initiative, so their capability matters most.
The coaching approach asks structured questions to help managers reason through a situation rather than giving them the solution.
HR must still intervene directly in legal, safeguarding, serious employee relations and significant organisational risk matters.
Management development should be an ongoing process using real workplace situations, not a one-off training event.

modules.reading: The article is about the people side of management: how managers handle performance, conflict and feedback, how they relate to HR and to their teams, and how employees choose whom to go to with a concern. Viewed through PWO, the issue is the capability of managers and the formal and informal structure of who decides what. A student of this module should care because the article links individual skill, feedback and performance management, power and dependence between HR and line managers, and the design of decision rights and escalation routes.

The article treats coaching as a leadership development approach: HR should develop managers' judgement rather than substitute for it. This raises questions about how leaders should adapt their style to the readiness of the person they lead, and about how developing leaders differs from directing them. Leadership students should see the article as a practical case of developing leaders through real situations, with the risk of over-directing managers who need to build their own judgement.

The article argues that HR should be measured by what it no longer has to fix, which is a point about performance measurement and value creation. It challenges the idea that a high volume of activity shows influence, and proposes measures that look at earlier and more appropriate handling of problems. Strategy students can see the article as an example of how a support function might build a measurement system that connects its work to wider organisational goals such as long-term growth and workforce capability.

applications.concept: Performance management and feedback
applications.theory: Performance management is a continuing process of setting expectations, monitoring performance, giving feedback and developing people, rather than an annual event. Feedback is most useful when it is timely, specific and focused on behaviour and outcomes that the person can act on. Managers who avoid difficult feedback let problems grow, which weakens both performance and the employee's trust in the process.
applications.link: The article describes managers who avoid difficult performance conversations and situations that could have been dealt with weeks earlier, which is the timeliness problem that performance management is meant to prevent. Its coaching questions about what has already been said and what the manager is worried about map onto the preparation stage of a feedback conversation, where evidence and expected outcomes are set out first. The author's view that performance conversations are development opportunities corresponds to treating feedback as a development tool rather than a disciplinary event. Where the article suggests that HR should help managers work through what evidence exists and what a fair outcome would look like, it describes the preparation that effective feedback requires.
applications.critique: The article treats avoidance as a gap in capability, but feedback avoidance can also come from workload pressure, unclear standards, weak organisational support or fear of conflict, and coaching alone may not address these. Feedback theory also suggests that the quality of the relationship and the employee's perception of fairness matter as much as the manager's skill.
applications.practice: A manager facing an avoided performance problem should first record specific evidence and agree the outcome they want, then hold a timely conversation focused on observable behaviour. HR can coach them through this preparation, and the organisation should set regular check-ins so that small issues are raised before they become formal.

applications.concept: French and Raven's bases of power, with resource dependence theory (Pfeffer and Salancik)
applications.theory: French and Raven identify five bases of power: legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent. Resource dependence theory holds that power accrues to those who control scarce, critical resources that others need, so that dependence on a particular unit or person shifts power towards it. A unit that is consulted on every problem becomes a critical resource for others.
applications.link: When HR becomes the default solver, managers depend on it for expertise and for the handling of difficult issues, which gives HR expert power and makes the manager's own legitimate authority less visible. The article notes that employees bypass their line manager and go to HR, which means the manager's referent power over the team weakens. The author's proposal to coach managers and clarify escalation boundaries is an attempt to reduce that dependence and restore the manager's legitimate and expert authority.
applications.critique: Resource dependence explains how power shifts, but not whether HR seeks it, and the article assumes that HR is simply being pulled in by managers. Lukes's third dimension of power suggests that dependence can be sustained by shared assumptions about who should handle problems, so changing behaviour may need changes to norms as well as to escalation rules.
applications.practice: HR should map which decisions are currently taken centrally and why, then return clearly defined decisions to line managers with the expertise and support they need. The organisation should publish escalation criteria so that managers and employees both understand when HR involvement is expected.

applications.concept: Situational leadership (Hersey and Blanchard)
applications.theory: Situational leadership holds that the effective leader adapts their style to the development level of the person being led, which depends on both competence and commitment. Directing suits low competence and commitment, coaching suits moderate competence with low confidence, supporting suits high competence with variable confidence, and delegating suits high competence and commitment. The leader's task is to match the style to the follower's readiness on each task.
applications.link: The article's advice to ask questions before offering wording or taking over matches the coaching style, which fits a manager who has the ability to handle a situation but lacks confidence or practice. The author also says that some situations need direct HR intervention, which corresponds to the directing style where competence on a specific issue is low or risk is high. Treating each difficult issue separately, as the article implies, reflects the task-specific nature of readiness in the model.
applications.critique: Situational leadership has been criticised for weak empirical support, for vague definitions of readiness, and for the way it labels people. The article also does not describe how HR would assess a manager's readiness, so applying the model in practice would depend on judgement the article does not specify.
applications.practice: HR business partners should assess a manager's readiness for each type of issue, such as a first performance conversation or a dispute between team members, and select a coaching, supporting or directing response accordingly. The aim should be to move the manager towards delegation over time, so that HR's involvement reduces as the manager's capability grows.

applications.concept: The balanced scorecard (Kaplan and Norton)
applications.theory: The balanced scorecard measures performance from four linked perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth. Its aim is to avoid over-reliance on financial measures by linking operational and capability measures to long-term strategic goals. Each perspective should have a few measures that show whether the organisation is building the capability it needs.
applications.link: The article argues that HR should measure whether problems are handled earlier and at the right level, not how many consultations it handles, which fits the internal process perspective of the scorecard. Increasing manager capability is a learning and growth measure, and the author links fewer avoidable escalations to better employee experience and to freeing HR for workforce planning and organisational design. The scorecard would therefore link HR's own activity to the organisation's strategic objectives.
applications.critique: Fewer escalations can conceal problems rather than solve them, if managers avoid raising issues or employees stop speaking up. A scorecard that rewards low escalation numbers could therefore encourage suppression, so the measures need to be checked against employee voice and outcome data.
applications.practice: HR should choose a small set of measures, such as the proportion of performance concerns addressed by the line manager within an agreed time, the number of managers who have completed coaching, and employee survey responses on whether they trust their manager with concerns. These should be reviewed alongside escalations to test that low volumes reflect real capability rather than silence.

caseStudy.scenario: A large organisation's HR team handles most difficult people issues, from avoided performance conversations to disputes between team members. Managers return to HR repeatedly with similar problems, and some employees take concerns directly to HR rather than to their line manager. The HR director wants to reposition the function so that it works more strategically, while still protecting the organisation from legal and serious risk.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate whether HR should coach line managers through everyday people problems rather than resolving them on their behalf, and advise the HR director on how the function should change.
evidence: The article states that HR is often the first port of call for difficult people issues, and that this can leave managers less capable and HR less strategic.
The author notes that employees may bypass their line manager and go to HR, which erodes manager confidence over time.
The article argues that managers shape how supported, engaged and valued people feel more than any policy or HR initiative does.
The article says a high volume of escalations is not necessarily a sign of influence, and suggests measuring whether problems are handled earlier and at the right level.
plan: Identify which problems are everyday and which need direct HR intervention, using the article's distinction between legal, safeguarding, serious employee relations and significant risk matters.
Explain the performance management problem: avoided and delayed feedback, and the need for timely, evidence-based conversations as set out in performance management and feedback theory.
Analyse why managers are dependent on HR using French and Raven's bases of power and resource dependence, and show how this weakens the manager's legitimate and referent authority.
Use situational leadership to explain how HR should match its coaching or directing response to each manager's readiness, and recognise that the model's empirical support is limited.
Propose clear decision rights and escalation criteria, and a balanced scorecard of measures that test whether problems are handled earlier and by the right person without suppressing employee voice.
Recommend a phased approach in which HR coaches managers on everyday issues, retains direct control for high-risk matters, and reviews outcomes over time.
pitfalls: Presenting the article's views as proven: it is practitioner opinion and does not supply data on outcomes, so the evaluation should test its claims rather than accept them.
Recommending that HR withdraw from all difficult issues, which ignores the article's explicit exceptions for legal, safeguarding and serious risk matters.

alsoConsider: McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that HR should coach line managers through people problems rather than resolve them on their behalf. Draw on theories of power, performance management and leadership development in your answer.
outline: Define coaching and direct intervention, and identify the types of issue for which each is appropriate, with reference to legal and safeguarding risk.
Explain how dependence on HR shifts power away from line managers, using French and Raven and resource dependence, and how this affects employee behaviour.
Evaluate the proposal against performance management and situational leadership theory, noting the limits of the evidence and the risk that low escalation numbers conceal problems.

articles.title: How Boards Detect and Prevent Internal Misconduct
articles.takeaway: The supplied text is only a short publisher's abstract, so it supports a note on the subject (boards detecting and preventing internal misconduct) rather than on specific findings. Read through PWO theory, the subject is mainly about culture, power and formal and informal structure, and it should be checked against the full excerpt before use in assessed work.
articles.summary: The source is an excerpt from the Harvard Business Review Board Member's Handbook, and its title indicates that it deals with how boards detect and prevent internal misconduct. The text supplied is only that short description, so it reports no findings, methods, cases or figures. The points below rest on the title and on what the relevant theories would lead a student to look for, and they should be checked against the full excerpt before being cited as evidence.
keyPoints: The subject is the board's role in detecting and preventing misconduct that comes from inside the organisation.
The supplied text gives no findings, methods or examples, so no claims about what boards actually do can be drawn from it.
Misconduct inside an organisation can be looked at as a question of culture, of power and information flows, and of how formal structures relate to informal practice.
Boards depend on information from management, so the people they oversee control much of what the board can see.
The source is a handbook excerpt, so it is likely to be practical guidance rather than an academic study; treat its advice as the publisher's view, not established evidence.

modules.reading: Read through People, Work and Organisations, the subject is how an organisation's culture, power relations and formal and informal structures allow or prevent misconduct, and how a governing body can see into them. Unit 7 explains the dark side of strong cultures, in which shared norms can suppress dissent or normalise wrongdoing. Unit 5 on power and politics explains why boards that rely on management for information may see only what those managers choose to show. A student should care because the title points to controls that a board can design, but the module suggests that the people and culture behind those controls decide whether they work.

Read through Leadership Theory and Practice, the subject raises questions about ethics and responsibility at the top of the organisation. A board sets the tone for executives and is accountable for the conduct of the people it appoints, which connects to ethical and responsible leadership. The module asks what it means for leaders to take responsibility for the behaviour of those who follow them. A student should care because misconduct prevention is partly a question of whether leaders model and enforce the standards that the board sets.

applications.concept: The dark side of organisational culture (Unit 7 theory; links to Schein's levels of culture)
applications.theory: Strong organisational cultures can improve coordination, but they can also suppress dissent, normalise questionable behaviour and make people reluctant to challenge the group. Schein distinguishes visible artefacts, espoused values and basic underlying assumptions, and the gap between stated values and what people actually assume can conceal misconduct. A toxic or overly strong culture can therefore make misconduct hard to detect even when formal controls exist.
applications.link: The title frames misconduct as something arising inside the organisation, which points to the cultural layer rather than to individual rule-breaking alone. A board that reads only formal artefacts, such as codes of conduct and policy documents, sees the espoused values but may miss the assumptions that govern what people actually do. Mapping the excerpt onto Schein's model suggests that detection depends on looking beneath the written standards. The supplied abstract does not say which methods the handbook recommends, so this mapping is a framework for analysis rather than a summary of the text.
applications.critique: Culture is difficult to observe and measure, and boards usually receive a filtered picture from management, so the diagnosis may itself be shaped by the culture under review. Treating culture as a single thing that can be managed also underplays its subcultures and the way different groups within the organisation experience it differently.
applications.practice: A board seeking to detect misconduct should combine formal controls with direct evidence about culture, such as staff surveys, exit interviews, and conversations with managers beyond the executive team. It should compare the stated values with the behaviours that are rewarded or tolerated in practice, and treat gaps between the two as a warning sign.

applications.concept: Lukes's three dimensions of power
applications.theory: Lukes distinguishes three dimensions of power: overt decision-making power, control over the agenda that decides which issues are raised, and the power to shape people's preferences so that they do not voice grievances. The second and third dimensions are the least visible, because they work by keeping certain issues out of view. Power can therefore be exercised through what is never put on the board's agenda.
applications.link: Boards depend on the executives they oversee for the information that reaches them, which gives management control over the agenda in Lukes's second sense. If misconduct is prevented or hidden by controlling what is reported, the board's oversight may be limited by the same power relations it is supposed to monitor. The title's focus on detection suggests that boards need to look at what is kept off their agenda as well as at what is presented to them. The supplied text does not describe such dynamics, so this link is an analytical application.
applications.critique: Lukes's framework is abstract and can be hard to apply to a specific board without evidence about who controls information and why. Some observers argue that boards can be given independent sources of information, such as internal audit and whistleblowing channels, which would reduce the effect of agenda control, so the power of management is not absolute.
applications.practice: A board should identify its independent sources of information, such as internal audit, direct access to staff and external advisers, and check whether these reach it without passing through management. It should ask regularly which topics have not been raised, and why, and should set the agenda in a way that protects against the third dimension of power.

applications.concept: Formal and informal organisation
applications.theory: Every organisation has a formal structure of reporting lines, rules and procedures, and an informal organisation of networks, friendships and unwritten practices that shape how work really gets done. The informal organisation can support or undermine the formal rules. Misconduct often lies in the gap between the two, because people can follow the formal process while the informal network decides what is acceptable.
applications.link: The subject of detection and prevention implies that formal control systems, such as codes, reporting lines and audit procedures, exist but may not reveal everything that happens. Mapping the excerpt onto this theory suggests that boards need to test whether the formal reporting structure matches the informal networks through which information and norms actually move. The abstract does not say whether the handbook takes this view, so the connection is an application of the theory to the title.
applications.critique: The formal and informal distinction can be overstated, since informal networks are sometimes a legitimate way to get things done and may not be a source of misconduct. Mapping informal networks is also difficult and can be seen as intrusive, which may create its own resistance from staff.
applications.practice: A board or its committee should ask for information on how reporting lines work in practice, including whether employees raise concerns through formal channels or informal ones, and whether whistleblowing routes operate independently of the line management being reported on. It should then compare what it learns with the formal structure and close any gaps it finds.

applications.concept: Ethical and responsible leadership
applications.theory: Ethical and responsible leadership concerns how leaders set and maintain moral standards in their organisations, both through their own conduct and through the systems they put in place. It holds that leaders are responsible for the ethical climate and for the behaviour of those they influence, not only for their own actions. Ethical leadership is therefore expressed through what leaders reward, tolerate and punish.
applications.link: A board is itself a leadership body whose responsibilities include the conduct of the organisation's executives, and the title's concern with preventing internal misconduct places the question of ethical standards at the top. The excerpt's focus on detection and prevention suggests that ethical leadership at board level is judged partly by the systems it establishes and how it responds to warning signs. The supplied text does not describe any particular ethical standards or responses, so this application relies on the title and on the theory.
applications.critique: Ethical leadership is often described in aspirational terms that are hard to test, and a board's commitment to ethics can be undermined if directors are rewarded for short-term results that depend on weak controls. Critics also point out that codes of conduct can become a form of reputation management rather than a real commitment to change.
applications.practice: A board should set explicit ethical expectations for executives and tie them to how performance is assessed, and should ensure that concerns raised about senior people are investigated independently of those people. It should report on how it has responded to past concerns, so that the standards it sets are visibly enforced.

caseStudy.scenario: A listed company's board is told that a senior manager may have breached internal rules, and that the concern was raised informally before reaching the board. The board wants to understand why the issue was not picked up earlier by its formal controls. The company has a code of conduct, an internal audit function and a whistleblowing policy that most staff say they know about.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on how it could have detected and prevented this kind of internal misconduct, drawing on the theories of organisational culture, power and formal and informal organisation.
evidence: The publication is an excerpt from the Harvard Business Review Board Member's Handbook, and its stated subject is how boards detect and prevent internal misconduct.

The supplied text is only the publisher's short description and reports no specific findings, methods or cases, so any evidence drawn from it should be cited as the subject of the source rather than as a result.
The title frames misconduct as an internal matter, which gives the student a basis for analysing it through organisational structures, culture and power relations.
plan: Define internal misconduct in organisational terms and note that the board's task is both to detect it and to prevent it, drawing on the handbook's stated subject.

Apply Schein's levels of culture to the scenario, comparing the written code of conduct with the assumptions that actually guided behaviour, and identify the dark side of strong culture as a possible reason the concern was delayed.
Apply Lukes's three dimensions of power to explain how management control over information may have limited what reached the board, and how the agenda may have kept the issue out of view.
Apply the formal and informal organisation to show where the informal concern moved outside the reporting and whistleblowing channels, and why the formal controls did not pick it up.

Recommend that the board establish independent information sources, test culture directly, reconcile formal and informal reporting, and set clear ethical expectations for senior managers, linking each recommendation to the theory that supports it.
pitfalls: Presenting the handbook's advice as established evidence, when the supplied text reports only its subject and no findings.
Treating the code of conduct and audit function as proof that controls were adequate, without examining how the informal organisation and power relations affected them.

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that internal misconduct is best prevented by formal board controls, rather than by understanding the culture, power relations and informal structures of the organisation.
outline: Explain the role of the board in detecting and preventing internal misconduct, and why formal controls alone may be insufficient.
Apply the dark side of culture and Lukes's dimensions of power to show how misconduct can persist despite formal systems, supporting each point with a clear example.
Evaluate the limits of these approaches and reach a reasoned judgement about what boards should prioritise.

articles.title: Nvidia's Asian Supply Chain Prepares for Life after Huang
articles.takeaway: The sudden exit of a chief executive whose personal relationships and vision had tied a supplier network together shows that suppliers can depend on one person rather than on the institution, so succession and relationship continuity become supply chain and change-management risks.
articles.summary: The article reports that Nvidia's partners and suppliers across Asia, including in Taiwan and South Korea, are reassessing their plans after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on 12 November, four days after the board had expressed confidence in him, following reports of two extramarital affairs. The chief financial officer, Colette Kress, was named interim CEO. Suppliers credit Huang's frequent visits, personal ties and ability to commit the firm to large investments and technology targets, and they fear a successor may be less aggressive in securing capacity or less accessible. Analysts disagree on the effects: one expects slower ecosystem investment and a loss of product clarity that could help rivals, while an investor argues that chips due in the next year or two are already designed and in production and that customers' spending does not depend on who runs the firm. The article is short news reporting and gives no data on how the supply chain will change.
keyPoints: Huang resigned suddenly on 12 November after reports of personal conduct, having been backed by the board on 8 November; the lede calls it an ouster, but the body describes a resignation.
Colette Kress, the CFO, became interim CEO on the day of the resignation.
Suppliers including TSMC, Foxconn and Wistron were built into Nvidia's network through Huang's frequent visits, and he reportedly planned about $150 billion of investment in Taiwan in a year.
A Taiwan supplier executive fears expansion could slow if a successor is slower to commit manufacturing capacity; the executive asked to remain anonymous.
A South Korean chip company official values Huang's accessibility and asks whether a successor would keep the same favourable relationship.

modules.reading: This is a case of a leader whose vision and risk-taking shaped commitments across a wide partner network, and the article shows what happens when that leader leaves suddenly. Leadership theory asks which of Huang's qualities, such as an inspiring technical vision, personal attention to partners and willingness to commit resources, can be passed on and which are tied to the individual. The reason given for the exit is personal conduct rather than performance, which raises questions for the module's work on ethics and responsibility, though the article does not develop them. Students should care because the case tests whether leadership effectiveness is a property of a person, of relationships or of the wider system.

In PWO terms, this is a leadership succession that changes where influence sits in an organisation and its network. Much of Huang's authority appears to have rested on personal credibility, visibility and relationships rather than on his formal post, so the question for partners is whether that influence transfers with the role. The departure is a sudden trigger for change that will move Nvidia and its partners through an interim period under a caretaker CEO. Students should care because it shows how power, culture and change interact when one individual has become the public face of an organisation.

From the buyer-supplier perspective, Nvidia holds a powerful position over suppliers that commit capacity on the strength of expected orders. One supplier fears that expansion will slow if a successor does not commit capacity quickly, which shows that supplier investment rests on the buyer's confidence and intentions. Students should care because the article shows the risk of relying on a relationship held by one person rather than on contracts or institutional ties.

The article describes a concentrated supply network spanning Taiwan foundries, Korean memory suppliers and customers in China, where order visibility and capacity investment depend on decisions at the focal firm. Analysts disagree on whether a change of direction would slow execution or leave rivals room to catch up, which is a question about the resilience of a network built around one buyer. Students should care because it shows that the focal firm's decisions on capacity and order commitments are a supply chain risk in their own right.

applications.concept: French and Raven's bases of power
applications.theory: French and Raven identified five bases of power: legitimate (from position), reward, coercive, expert (from knowledge or skill) and referent (from identification and personal liking). Power can rest on the person as well as the role, and the bases differ in how easily they transfer to a successor. Students should be able to say which base is at stake in a leadership change and why that affects continuity.
applications.link: Huang's influence, as described in the article, rests largely on expert and referent bases: suppliers credit his technical judgement in turning engineers' ideas into committed products, and Korean partners value his accessibility and the roadmap he sketched personally for Naver's founder. The Korean official's question about whether a successor would keep the same favourable relationship suggests that referent power does not pass automatically with the job. The formal legitimate power of the CEO post now belongs to the interim CEO, who is the CFO, so the partners' relationships are being tested against a different basis of influence. The Taiwan executive's remark that a successor may not be as aggressive points to the expert and referent bases being in doubt.
applications.critique: French and Raven describe the bases of power but say little about how they transfer or how a power holder should replace them, and the article's supplier comments may overstate personal power because Nvidia's chips are in production and its scale gives it leverage regardless of who leads it.
applications.practice: A board appointing or confirming an interim leader should identify which relationships depend on personal referent or expert power and move them onto institutional channels, such as named account teams, joint steering committees and written capacity commitments. It should also let the new leader meet key partners early, so that trust is seen to rest on the organisation as well as the individual.

applications.concept: Bridges's transition model
applications.theory: William Bridges separated the external change event from the internal psychological transition that people go through. The transition has three phases: an ending, in which people let go of the old situation; a neutral zone, a confused in-between period in which new arrangements are tried; and a new beginning, when people commit to new ways of working. Managers need to plan for each phase, not only for the change itself.
applications.link: The sudden resignation is an ending for suppliers and partners who built their working relationships around Huang, and the article shows them moving quickly from confidence to reassessment, with the board's backing on 8 November reversed four days later. The period under interim CEO Colette Kress is a neutral zone: suppliers are assessing what the change means, Korean firms are reviewing their ties, and Chinese AI firms are securing access in case regulation tightens. The article contains no sign yet of a new beginning, though the investor's comment that roadmaps and customer spending are fixed suggests that some stakeholders already expect continuity.
applications.critique: Bridges's model is largely an individual and group account of psychological transition and does not explain the external pressures, such as possible US curbs on remote access, that drive many of the behaviours reported in the article. It also assumes that a transition is needed, whereas the investor view suggests that for some stakeholders the change may have little practical effect.
applications.practice: Nvidia and its partners should name what is ending, such as direct access to Huang, and state clearly what continues, such as roadmaps and committed capacity. They should then set a timetable for the neutral zone, for example joint roadmap reviews with the new leadership, so that partners can move to commitment rather than hedge.

applications.concept: Transformational leadership (Burns; Bass)
applications.theory: Burns contrasted transactional leadership, which exchanges rewards for performance, with transformational leadership, which raises followers' awareness of shared goals and motivates them to go beyond self-interest. Bass developed four components: idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration. Bass and Steidlmeier later distinguished authentic transformational leaders from pseudo-transformational ones who use vision to serve their own interests.
applications.link: The article describes Huang taking engineers' possibilities and turning them into products the whole company commits resources to, which maps onto intellectual stimulation and inspirational motivation in Bass's terms. The Korean partner's praise for his accessibility matches individualised consideration, and the analyst's remark that his competitors are forced to follow suggests that his vision spreads through the industry. The article's account of his personal conduct is outside the leadership dimensions, but it raises the question of whether the vision and the individual can be separated.
applications.critique: Transformational leadership is often criticised for its heroic and charismatic emphasis, which can encourage dependence on one person; the theory does not explain how a vision becomes embedded in an organisation after its founder or champion leaves, and the article shows an industry relying heavily on one individual.
applications.practice: A board should separate the vision from the person by documenting strategic priorities and decision rights, building a senior team that shares the vision, and using the interim period to check whether partner relationships have been institutionalised. Board members should also judge whether the successor can give the same individual attention to key partners.

applications.concept: Power in buyer-supplier relationships (Cox)
applications.theory: Cox argues that the balance of power in buyer-supplier relationships depends on relative dependence: the party that relies more on the relationship, and has fewer alternatives, has less power. Purchasing strategy should therefore map who depends on whom, and whether that dependence is symmetric, before choosing a sourcing and relationship approach.
applications.link: Nvidia buys from concentrated suppliers such as TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron and SK Hynix, and suppliers commit capacity on the strength of expected orders, which is the dependence Cox describes. The Taiwan executive's fear that expansion will slow if the successor is less quick to commit capacity shows how supplier investment is tied to the buyer's intentions. The Korean partners' question about whether ties will survive a leadership change suggests that Nvidia also depends on suppliers, particularly for high-bandwidth memory produced in South Korea.
applications.critique: Cox's analysis is largely static and treats power as a balance of resources; it does not capture trust built through personal relationships, and the article suggests that the relationships may matter as much as the formal dependence. It also gives limited weight to the possibility that suppliers can find alternative customers in the AI chip market.
applications.practice: Nvidia's purchasing team should map dependence on each key supplier and reduce single-person dependence through long-term capacity agreements, joint investment plans and clear escalation routes. Supplier terms should rest on contracts and documented commitments rather than on the personal assurances of the chief executive.

caseStudy.scenario: A US designer of specialised AI processors has announced the sudden resignation of its chief executive after reports of personal conduct, four days after the board had expressed confidence in him. Its suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea have committed to expansion on the strength of his strategy and personal relationships, and the company has named its chief financial officer as interim chief executive. Some suppliers fear a successor will be less aggressive in securing manufacturing capacity, while analysts disagree on whether product plans and customer spending will change in the short term.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on how the company should manage the leadership transition so that its suppliers, partners and internal organisation maintain their commitment. Draw on theories of power, organisational change and leadership.
evidence: The chief executive resigned suddenly on 12 November, after the board had backed him on 8 November.
A Taiwan supplier executive said expansion could slow if a successor was less quick to commit manufacturing capacity, and asked to remain anonymous.
A South Korean chip company official said the key question was whether a successor would keep the same favourable relationship with the company.

One analyst warned that any slowdown in execution or loss of product roadmap clarity could give rivals room to catch up, while an investor said the chips due in the next year or two are already designed and in production.
plan: Diagnose the change as a sudden leadership succession and frame the transition using Bridges's three phases of ending, neutral zone and new beginning.

Analyse the source of the chief executive's influence using French and Raven, separating legitimate power from referent and expert power and identifying which relationships would not transfer automatically.
Assess stakeholder dependence using Cox's power analysis, distinguishing suppliers that depend on the company's orders from the company's own dependence on key memory suppliers.

Evaluate the vision and leadership style using Bass's transformational leadership, and identify which elements of the vision need to be institutionalised in strategy, teams and contracts rather than held by one person.
Weigh the short-term and long-term risks, noting that near-term products may be fixed while roadmap clarity and partner confidence are more exposed.
Recommend a transition plan with named continuity contacts, documented capacity commitments, early meetings between the new leadership and key partners, and a clear timetable for the neutral zone.
pitfalls: Describing the event as a settled dismissal when the article reports a resignation, or treating the affairs as the main business issue rather than the consequences for relationships and capacity.
Assuming that the chief executive was irreplaceable without testing this against the article's evidence that near-term chip production and customer plans are already fixed.

alsoConsider: Weber's charismatic authority and the routinisation of charisma

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that the sudden departure of a charismatic chief executive poses a lasting threat to an organisation's relationships with its suppliers and partners, and explain how leaders can reduce that risk.
outline: Explain how the chief executive's influence rested on personal referent and expert power rather than on the legitimate authority of the post, using French and Raven.
Apply Bridges's transition model to the interim period, identifying the ending, the neutral zone and the conditions for a new beginning, and assess whether the dependence is real or overstated.
Conclude with recommendations that institutionalise relationships through contracts, shared teams and clear communication, drawing on transformational leadership and Cox's power analysis.

articles.title: What Your Balance Sheet Says About Supply Chain Execution
articles.takeaway: The cash conversion cycle works as a cross-functional scorecard: trapped working capital is a symptom of broken handoffs between sales, planning, procurement, operations and finance, and it stays fixed only when the management system itself changes.
articles.summary: Zeffiro argues that inventory, receivables and payables reveal how well an operating model works. He cites J.P. Morgan's Working Capital Index, reported in Forbes in June 2026, which puts roughly $707 billion of cash in S&P 1,500 companies tied up in working capital, up 40% on pre-pandemic levels, with cash conversion cycles lengthening by an average of 2.4 days. He locates the cause at the seams between functions: optimistic sales forecasts, defensive buying and production scheduled around both build stock, unvetted commercial terms and unowned disputes stretch receivables, and payables are stretched to compensate for both. Treasury-led programmes harvest these symptoms through one-off actions that fade once the task force disbands, whereas lasting gains come from one integrated forecast, joint accountability and cash variances reviewed in the weekly management cadence. He describes an industrial biotechnology company whose total inventory fell 54% after it rebuilt its forecasting-to-fulfilment model, and advises CEOs to judge the trend over eight to twelve quarters and to treat deterioration as a management system finding.
keyPoints: Inventory, receivables and payables reveal whether the operating model integrates or fragments, and they are visible on the balance sheet before the organisation names the problem.
Inventory builds when forecasting, procurement and production work from different assumptions, so buffer stock becomes a measure of how far functions distrust each other's numbers.
Receivables stretch when commercial terms are agreed without operational vetting and when no single owner spans sales, service and finance.
Stretching payables compensates for cash trapped elsewhere but can degrade supplier performance, which then feeds back into inventory.
One-off working capital programmes change the numbers without changing the decision rights, forecasting cadence and accountability that produce them, so gains erode within about a year.

modules.reading: The article is about how structure, processes and management routines shape behaviour across functions. Each function pursues its own metrics rationally, so the organisation's result depends on how work crosses the boundaries between sales, planning, procurement, operations and finance. For a PWO student the lesson is that poor outcomes can come from design and routines rather than individual failings, and that change which alters only the numbers, not the systems behind them, tends not to last. It bears on organisation design, intergroup conflict and sustaining organisational change.

Working capital is the core subject here: inventory, receivables and payables together form the cash conversion cycle, which measures the days between paying for inputs and collecting cash from customers. The article treats the cycle as a diagnostic of operations rather than a treasury lever, and argues that stretching payables is a patch that harms supplier performance. A finance student should see why the components must be decomposed and read alongside operating drivers before any judgement on liquidity is made.

The article treats forecasting, procurement and production as one linked system and measures its performance in cash terms. The inventory build that comes from distorted forecasts is a supply chain integration problem, not just a working capital one. Students of SCM should see that the gains come from shared planning and better demand information rather than from pushing stock or payment burdens onto other parties.

applications.concept: Galbraith's Star Model
applications.theory: Galbraith's Star Model holds that organisational performance depends on five design choices: strategy, structure, processes, rewards and people. These elements must be aligned, and a change to one usually requires matching changes to the others. Structure allocates decision rights, while processes and reward systems determine how work flows and which behaviour is recognised.
applications.link: The article's problem is an alignment failure: sales forecasts optimistically, supply chain buys defensively and production schedules around both, so the processes and measures in different functions point in different directions. The author's remedy of one integrated forecast that sales, operations and finance are jointly accountable to changes the processes and decision rights rather than the treasury targets. Terms set without operational input show decision rights sitting with people who do not bear the consequences of those terms. The biotechnology case, where demand planning, production and distribution were connected through integrated systems, shared targets and clear accountability, shows the star's demand that several points change together.
applications.critique: The model is a design framework rather than a theory of how change happens, so it says little about why functions resist alignment when it threatens their own measures and influence. It also gives limited attention to the informal networks that often decide whether a cross-functional process works in practice.
applications.practice: A CEO applying the model would map each element against the cash cycle, asking who sets commercial terms, who owns the integrated forecast and which bonuses reward stock levels. The CEO would then realign the conflicting points, for example by requiring joint sign-off on terms and linking part of sales and operations incentives to cash conversion, before relying on new systems.

applications.concept: Kotter's eight-step model of change
applications.theory: Kotter's eight-step model sets out a sequence for leading transformation: create urgency, build a guiding coalition, develop a vision, communicate it, empower broad-based action, generate short-term wins, consolidate gains and anchor new approaches in culture. Kotter warns that declaring victory early allows old habits to return. The final steps are about making change permanent by embedding it in culture and routine systems.
applications.link: The article describes the typical arc of a treasury-led programme: a diagnostic, targets, a task force pushing for two or three quarters, then gains quietly eroding within a year. This matches Kotter's warning about the danger of short-term wins that are not consolidated. The author's claim that the programme changed the numbers without changing the machinery corresponds to the missing anchoring step, because new behaviour never became part of routine management. The biotechnology company's sustained gains came when its disciplines were embedded in everyday management, which is the consolidation and anchoring Kotter describes.
applications.critique: Kotter's model is largely linear and prescriptive, drawn from case observation rather than systematic evidence, and it can understate political resistance and the way small routine changes can become permanent without a formal culture programme. Its emphasis on leaders may also miss the bottom-up management practices the article credits.
applications.practice: A manager would make the working capital metrics part of the weekly operating review, with named owners across sales, operations and finance and with cash variances treated like output variances. Before the programme formally ends, the manager would write the new decision rights and forecast ownership into the standing management system, so the gains do not depend on a task force.

applications.concept: Working capital management and the cash conversion cycle
applications.theory: The cash conversion cycle measures the number of days between paying suppliers for inputs and collecting cash from customers, calculated as days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding minus days payables outstanding. A lengthening cycle means more cash is tied up in operations, which reduces liquidity and increases the need for external funding. Managing it involves reducing inventory and receivable days and, with care, extending payables, since stretching suppliers can damage supply performance.
applications.link: The article's reported 2.4 day lengthening of the cycle and its $707 billion of trapped liquidity are direct measures of this metric across large US companies. The author's three-part breakdown corresponds to the components of the cycle: rising inventory maps onto days inventory outstanding, stretching receivables onto days sales outstanding, and payables used as a lever onto days payables outstanding. The argument that payables stretching degrades supplier performance and feeds back into inventory shows the components interacting, so they cannot be managed as independent levers. The author also advises reading the trend over eight to twelve quarters rather than the level against peers, which is the interpretive approach a finance student should adopt.
applications.critique: The cash conversion cycle is a blended average that can conceal offsetting movements, such as a falling payables figure masking an improvement in receivables, and it can be flattered by pressing suppliers. The article's causal claims about functional behaviour are the author's inferences from experience rather than measured relationships.
applications.practice: A finance manager would calculate inventory, receivable and payable days separately by product line, site and customer group, and compare each with its own trend. Before recommending changes to payment terms, the manager would test the effect on supplier performance and check whether any payables gain is a genuine improvement rather than a transfer of cost upstream.

applications.concept: The bullwhip effect (Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang)
applications.theory: The bullwhip effect describes how modest fluctuations in customer demand grow as orders move upstream through a supply chain, producing large swings in inventory. Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang identified causes including demand forecast updating, order batching, price fluctuations and shortage gaming, and argued that sharing demand information and coordinating decisions reduces the distortion. Information sharing is therefore a central remedy.
applications.link: The article describes sales forecasting optimistically, procurement buying defensively and production scheduling around both, which is a chain of distorted signals that inflates stock. The author's insistence on one integrated forecast that sales, operations and finance share applies the information-sharing remedy directly. The 54% inventory fall at the biotechnology company after demand planning, production and distribution were connected is consistent with that remedy, although the article gives no decomposition of which causes were removed.
applications.critique: Bullwhip research is largely based on modelled multi-stage chains, whereas the article's distortions are internal and driven by incentives and distrust, which information sharing alone may not resolve. The source of the distortion may be behavioural, so cross-functional governance and incentives may matter more than the systems themselves.
applications.practice: A supply chain manager would trace order variance against sales demand for the product lines where inventory is building, and identify the stage at which variance grows. The manager would then agree a shared demand plan with sales and finance, with performance judged on forecast accuracy as well as on stock levels.

caseStudy.scenario: A listed industrial group has run two treasury-led working capital programmes in three years, and each time inventory and receivables improved for two or three quarters before drifting back.
