Stock is building in several product lines, and the sales and supply chain teams disagree about forecasts and about the terms agreed for large customers. The board has asked for a plan that will hold the cash gains after the next programme ends, and the CFO believes the problem lies in treasury discipline.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate why the working capital gains from the group's previous programmes have eroded, and advise the board on how to make the improvement last.
evidence: S&P 1,500 companies were holding about $707 billion of trapped liquidity, up 40% on pre-pandemic levels, with cash conversion cycles lengthened by an average of 2.4 days
An industrial biotechnology company rebuilt its forecasting-to-fulfilment model, connecting demand planning, production and distribution, and total inventory fell 54%
The gains at that company were sustained once the disciplines were embedded in routine management rather than left to a programme
The article's account of the usual arc: a diagnostic, targets, a task force for two or three quarters, then erosion within about a year as attention moves on
plan: Define the cash conversion cycle and decompose it into inventory days, receivable days and payable days to show where the cash is trapped (finance)
Diagnose the seams using Galbraith's Star Model, showing how strategy, structure, processes, rewards and people are misaligned across sales, planning, procurement and finance (PWO Unit 6)
Explain the erosion with Kotter's model, showing that short-term wins were not consolidated or anchored in routine management (PWO Unit 8)
Use the bullwhip effect to show how distorted forecast signals between sales and procurement create the inventory buffer and how information sharing addresses it (SCM)

Recommend a single integrated forecast with joint accountability, operational vetting of terms, cash variances reviewed in the weekly cadence and rewards aligned across functions, and assess the risks of stock-outs and supplier strain
pitfalls: Treating the 54% result at the biotechnology company as proof the approach works everywhere, when it is one reported case with no detail on method or counterfactual
Recommending tighter payment terms as a quick fix without noting that the article shows this degrades supplier performance and feeds back into inventory

alsoConsider: Lewin's three-step model and force field analysis

exam.question: Critically evaluate the claim that organisational change programmes fail to sustain performance because they alter outcomes without altering the structures, processes and routines that produce them. Illustrate your answer with reference to organisational design and change management theory.
outline: Define the claim and explain, using Galbraith's Star Model, how misaligned structures, processes and rewards can generate persistent poor outcomes
Apply Kotter's model to explain why short-term gains erode without consolidation and anchoring, using a real example
Critically evaluate the approach by considering the limits of rational design models, the role of functional politics and resistance, and whether embedding routines is always feasible

articles.title: Using Weather Forecasts to Sharpen Regional Demand Planning
articles.takeaway: A national demand plan built on history and national totals hides regional weather effects, so weather should be treated as a measurable demand input with a defined forecast horizon, matched to the decision it informs.
articles.summary: The article argues that one national plan cannot serve regions whose weather diverged sharply in the same year. Pest control rose 11.0% in the Northeast and fell 4.1% in the West, while mold and mildew prevention rose 47% in the Midwest and 31% in the Northeast after flooding. Because national averages offset regional gains and losses, performance looks unremarkable while inventory is in the wrong places, producing expedited freight, transfers and markdowns. The author identifies three weak planning inputs: last year's sales, national totals, and seasonal assumptions based on a calendar that is changing. He recommends matching weather horizons to decisions (long-range for facilities, 30 to 90 day outlooks for allocation and safety stock, two to six week forecasts for deployment), building regional forecasts, applying seasonal adjustments only to proven weather-sensitive categories, setting trigger thresholds, and evaluating post-season variance against weather.
keyPoints: A single national plan produced very different outcomes across four regions in the same year, leaving some retailers overstocked and others short.
Regional category results diverged: pest control rose 11.0% in the Northeast and fell 4.1% in the West; mold and mildew prevention rose 47% in the Midwest.
National averages hide regional misses because gains in one region offset losses in another, so an aggregate-accurate plan can still be wrong where stock sits.
Three planning inputs are weak: historical sales embed last year's weather, national totals mask regional differences, and seasonal calendars are becoming less reliable.
Forecast horizon should match the decision: long-range patterns for facility location, 30 to 90 day outlooks for regional allocation and safety stock, and two to six week forecasts for deployment.

modules.reading: The article is about demand and inventory management under uncertain, region-specific demand. Its central point is that an aggregated forecast disaggregated by historical share reproduces last year's conditions, so stock is deployed to the wrong markets. For SCM students it is a clear case of how forecasting horizon, pre-positioning, safety stock and responsiveness interact, and it gives a practical route to building resilience against environmental volatility.

In logistics terms, the costs described (expedited freight, inter-depot transfers and markdowns) are the symptoms of mismatched inventory across the distribution network. The article questions tiering distribution centres by volume alone, since a high-volume and a low-volume site can need different seasonal stock depending on weather-driven variability. Students of freight and warehouse management should see how network design, safety stock and pre-positioning respond to this kind of demand variability.

The article's contrast between one national plan and regional forecasts is a question of organisation design: how much decision authority is centralised, and how units are integrated. The changing climate is an external trigger that the existing planning process was not built to absorb, which links to change management. Students of People, Work and Organisations can use contingency theory to explain why a structure that suits a stable environment fails when conditions diverge by region.

Weather is an environmental force that shapes demand differently in each market, which makes it a natural addition to an external environmental analysis. The article also shows that the same environmental trend matters on different time horizons, which affects how strategic and operational decisions should be timed. Strategy students can use it to show how an external factor is translated into a specific operational response.

applications.concept: Fisher's supply chain matrix (Fisher, 1997)
applications.theory: Fisher classifies products by demand predictability and life cycle, arguing that functional products with stable demand need efficient supply chains that minimise cost, while innovative products with unpredictable demand need responsive supply chains that can match supply to demand quickly. The choice of design should therefore follow the nature of demand uncertainty, not just the product type.
applications.link: The article shows that most household care categories are not weather-sensitive and can be planned on normal assumptions, while a handful of weather-sensitive categories move sharply by region. The pest control and mold prevention results illustrate demand that is unpredictable at regional level even though the product is functional. The author's advice to apply seasonal outlooks only where weather sensitivity is proven is a matrix-style segmentation of categories by predictability. The sharp contrast between metro and rural cold and flu sales also shows that predictability differs within one product category.
applications.critique: Fisher's binary treatment of products is a simplification, because weather-driven demand is better understood as a property of category, region and time together, which the matrix does not capture. Applying one label to a whole category could therefore mislead planners.
applications.practice: Classify each category and region combination by demand predictability using historical weather sensitivity. Apply a responsive approach with pre-positioning and fast deployment triggers to the sensitive combinations, and an efficient, low-buffer approach to the rest.

applications.concept: ABC inventory analysis and safety stock
applications.theory: ABC analysis ranks items or locations by value or volume so that management effort and control are focused on the most important ones. Safety stock is extra inventory held to absorb variability in demand and lead time, and it rises with demand variability and the risk of stockout, so it should be set for each location rather than as a flat share of volume.
applications.link: The article notes that most networks tier their distribution centres by volume, which can place Phoenix and Boston in one group and give them the same seasonal plan, even though their weather and demand variability differ. Because weather drives regional variability, the safety stock needed in each region depends on that variability, not on volume alone. The costs the article lists, including expedited freight, transfers and markdowns, are what happens when safety stock is positioned poorly. Pre-positioning based on 30 to 90 day outlooks is a direct way of adjusting safety stock before the season opens.
applications.critique: ABC classification by volume or value ignores demand variability, so a high-volume site with stable demand may be over-buffered while a lower-volume weather-exposed site is under-buffered. Safety stock formulas also assume demand is stable over the period, which a changing climate challenges.
applications.practice: Add a variability dimension to the ABC tiering, for example by classifying sites on both volume and weather-driven demand variance. Set regional safety stock levels for weather-sensitive categories from seasonal outlooks, and revisit them when the short-range forecast changes.

applications.concept: Mechanistic and organic structures (Burns and Stalker) and contingency theory (Lawrence and Lorsch)
applications.theory: Burns and Stalker describe mechanistic structures, with clear hierarchy, specialisation, formal rules and central decision making, as suited to stable environments, and organic structures, with flexible roles, lateral communication and decentralised decisions, as suited to unstable ones. Lawrence and Lorsch argue that greater environmental uncertainty requires more differentiation between units and stronger mechanisms for integrating them.
applications.link: A single national plan built on last year's sales and allocated by historical share is a mechanistic approach, applied to an environment that diverged by region. The four regional outcomes are the uncertainty the structure failed to absorb. The author's recommendation to build regional forecasts is a call for differentiation, and the trigger thresholds and post-season variance reviews are integration mechanisms that link regional and central planners. The article does not describe the internal structure of any company, so the link is to the planning design it implies rather than to observed organisational behaviour.
applications.critique: Contingency theory explains which structure fits which environment but says little about how to achieve the fit or about the costs of change. Centralised planning also gives scale economies and consistent control, and decentralising it may create coordination problems that the article does not address.
applications.practice: Give regional planners authority over allocation within central guardrails on budget and service levels. Create formal integration mechanisms, such as shared weather and sales dashboards, agreed thresholds for changing deployment, and a joint post-season review, so that regional sensing and central control work together.

applications.concept: PESTEL analysis
applications.theory: PESTEL scans the political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal factors that shape an organisation's external environment. It is used to identify which external forces will affect demand, costs and risk, and it is usually the first step before SWOT analysis and strategic choice.
applications.link: The article treats weather as an environmental factor that changes demand by region, with effects that appear in the South's warming winters and in the regional pattern of flooding and drought. The population shift to the South, cited in the article, is a social factor that interacts with the environmental one, so the two should be analysed together. The article's distinction between decades, months and weeks shows that the same environmental trend must be assessed over different horizons.
applications.critique: PESTEL is a checklist that treats each factor separately and presents a static picture, whereas the article's problem arises from interaction and timing. A PESTEL note on weather would need scenario analysis to show how the factor could play out in each region.
applications.practice: Add a regional weather dimension to the environmental part of the analysis and link it to population growth in the fastest-growing markets. Use scenarios for the main regions to test how far the current plan holds if conditions diverge again.

caseStudy.scenario: A national home-care products retailer buys for the whole country using one plan, built from last year's sales and allocated to regions by historical share. In one season its Northeast stores ran short of pest control lines while its Western stores held surplus stock, and it paid for expedited freight and transfers to correct the imbalance. The board has asked for a review of how demand planning is organised and controlled.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on whether demand planning should be centralised or devolved to regional teams, using organisation design and contingency theory.
evidence: Pest control sales rose 11.0% in the Northeast and fell 4.1% in the West in the same year.
Mold and mildew prevention rose 47% in the Midwest and 31% in the Northeast, the latter following flooding.
Cold and flu peak season sales fell 3.6% nationally, yet upper respiratory grew in the Mountain West, Texas, the Gulf Coast, the Carolinas and Florida.
Sales in the eight highest-density markets climbed 15.8% over three weeks, against 10.5% in rural markets, so metros indicated the wider trend.
plan: Diagnose the environment: show that regional demand was highly uncertain and varied by location, using the regional figures as evidence, and apply Burns and Stalker to classify the current planning structure as mechanistic.
Explain the fit problem: the central plan and its historical-share allocation suit a stable environment and fail when regions diverge, as Lawrence and Lorsch's contingency argument predicts.

Assess the need for differentiation: argue that regional teams need authority over allocation and forecasting because the environment differs by region, and identify which categories are weather-sensitive enough to justify this.

Design integration: specify the mechanisms that keep the organisation coherent, including agreed trigger thresholds, shared dashboards, central guardrails on budget and service, and a joint post-season variance review.
Link to decision horizons: assign long-range, seasonal and short-range weather inputs to the decisions each can inform, so responsibility is matched to information.
Recommend a hybrid structure with clear decision rights, justified by the contingency analysis and weighed against the loss of scale economies from decentralising.
pitfalls: Recommending full decentralisation without integration mechanisms or without weighing the costs of coordination and lost scale.
Describing the regional data without linking it to organisation design or to contingency theory, which is what the question asks for.

alsoConsider: Lean, agile and leagile supply chains (Christopher; Naylor)

exam.question: Critically evaluate the claim that organisations facing highly variable regional environments should decentralise their decision making. Use contingency theory and illustrate your answer with evidence from regional demand planning.
outline: Define contingency theory and the mechanistic and organic distinction, and explain how environmental uncertainty and differentiation relate.
Use regional demand evidence to show how a centralised plan can fail when conditions diverge by location, and assess whether decentralisation is the answer.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of decentralising, including integration mechanisms, scale economies and coordination, and conclude with a justified recommendation.

articles.title: Back-to-Back Million+ TEU Months at PoLA Set Record
articles.takeaway: Record container volumes at Los Angeles show strong demand and handling capacity, but volume alone cannot prove a durable competitive advantage, because much of the surge is driven by demand and trade policy outside the port's control.
articles.summary: The Port of Los Angeles handled about 1.03 million TEUs in October, its second-highest monthly total and the second month running above one million, following a September all-time record. The port reports nearly 5 million TEUs from June to October, its strongest five-month stretch. The port's executive attributes the volume to consumer spending, retailers restocking inventories, changes in trade policy and disruption on other global shipping routes, and presents speed, reliability and reach as reasons customers choose the port.
keyPoints: October's volume of about 1,026,872 TEUs is the port's second-highest monthly total ever, and the article says it follows September's all-time record.
It is the first time the port has exceeded one million TEUs in consecutive months, and the article says it reached that mark three times in the year.
From June to October the port handled nearly 5 million TEUs, described as its strongest five-month period.
The executive attributes the surge to consumer spending, inventory replenishment, trade policy changes and challenges on other global shipping routes.
The claim that no other US port has handled a million TEUs in one month is the port's own statement, and the article gives no independent evidence for it.

modules.reading: The article is about throughput at a container port, the basic output measure of a freight terminal, expressed in TEUs. In logistics terms the port is a node in a freight network, where ships, cranes, yard space and onward inland transport must absorb the flow, and a million-TEU month is a stress test of that whole system. A student should care because the article reports volume and capacity used, but not the service or cost performance delivered to users.

Port volume is a downstream signal of what buyers are ordering, so supply chain theory treats it as the end result of a longer chain of replenishment decisions. The article links the surge to retailers restocking and to shifting trade policy and rerouted shipping, which are classic sources of order amplification and disruption. It also shows a network responding to problems elsewhere, which raises resilience questions.

The port's executive presents speed, reliability and reach as the reasons customers choose Los Angeles, which is a claim about competitive advantage. In strategy terms the question is whether those features are valuable, rare and hard to copy, or whether they reflect location and carriers' routing choices that the port does not control. The article offers the claim without comparative data on rival ports, so it should be treated as the port's own view.

applications.concept: Total logistics cost and the cost-service trade-off
applications.theory: Logistics managers balance the total cost of moving and holding goods against the service level customers receive, and the two often pull in opposite directions. Total logistics cost includes transport, handling, inventory and the cost of poor service, so lowering one element can raise another. Speed and reliability are service outputs that require spare capacity to deliver.
applications.link: The port says customers value speed, reliability and reach, which are service outcomes rather than cost outcomes. Record months of around a million TEUs suggest the terminal is working close to its limits, where additional throughput often increases congestion and waiting times unless capacity has been added. The article reports no dwell times, berth waiting or cost per box, so the claimed service advantage cannot be checked against what it costs to deliver.
applications.critique: The trade-off model assumes cost and service can be measured on a common basis, which is hard in a port where costs fall on carriers, shippers and hauliers in different ways. A systems view would ask whether the binding constraint lies at the port or in the inland links that carry its cargo.
applications.practice: A port operator applying this framework should track total cost to shippers, including inland transport and delay, alongside volume. It should check whether volume gains are being bought with longer waits, and report on-time performance and dwell time as service measures.

applications.concept: The bullwhip effect (Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang)
applications.theory: Small changes in consumer demand can produce larger swings in orders as they move upstream, because each tier orders on the basis of the orders it receives and adds safety stock, batching or forecast error. The effect arises from distorted information about demand rather than from real demand change alone. Its amplitude grows the further upstream an order travels.
applications.link: The article says retailers were replenishing inventories while trade policy was changing, which is the kind of situation in which firms order ahead of need or pull stock forward to avoid future tariffs or shortages. That behaviour would push port throughput above underlying consumer demand, which the article also mentions as a driver. Three consecutive million-TEU months fit a pattern of bunched orders, although the article gives no inventory or order data to confirm it.
applications.critique: The bullwhip effect is usually explained by internal causes such as forecasting, batching and rationing, whereas the article points to an external policy shift, which is a different mechanism. Some of the surge may reflect genuine end demand, and port data alone cannot separate the two.
applications.practice: A port planning capacity should avoid extrapolating peak months. It should work with shipping lines and large retailers to share forecasts and order timing, so that a policy-driven rush is not mistaken for a lasting trend.

applications.concept: Supply chain risk management and resilience (Christopher and Peck)
applications.theory: Resilience is the ability of a supply network to resist disruption and return to stable operation, and it is built through redundancy, flexibility, visibility and collaboration. Christopher and Peck argue that risk should be assessed across the whole network and that networks must be designed for disruption as well as for efficiency.
applications.link: The article attributes part of the volume to challenges on other global shipping routes, which implies that cargo was diverted to Los Angeles when other routes were disrupted. The port therefore gained from a network-level disruption, and its throughput rose because of problems elsewhere. A resilience lens asks whether the port and its users now face concentration risk, since heavy reliance on one gateway exposes them if conditions there change.
applications.critique: The framework was written mainly from the standpoint of a single firm managing its own supply base, and applying it to a shared public gateway used by competing carriers is less straightforward. The article does not say how diverted cargo is distributed, so the resilience gain cannot be quantified.
applications.practice: A port authority or large shipper should map where its volume depends on a single route or gateway and then build contingency capacity or alternative routings. It should also monitor disruption on other routes as an early signal of diversion pressure.

applications.concept: The resource-based view and VRIO (Barney)
applications.theory: The resource-based view holds that sustained competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organised to be exploited, which is summarised as VRIO. A resource that meets all four tests can sustain above-average returns, whereas one that is only valuable tends to yield parity.
applications.link: The executive presents speed, reliability and reach as the reasons customers choose the port, and credits its partners and daily waterfront work. Under VRIO the test is whether these features are rare and inimitable. A port's physical position and its links to inland transport are hard to copy, which supports the claim, but the record volumes depend on demand and policy, which are not resources the port owns or controls.
applications.critique: VRIO was developed for firm-level resources, and ports are shared infrastructure whose advantages neighbouring ports can partly replicate. The article gives the port's own view and no evidence from rivals.
applications.practice: The port should separate the advantages it controls, such as capacity, productivity and inland connections, from those it does not. It should invest in the controllable ones and test its claims against rivals, for example by comparing dwell times, before presenting volume as proof of advantage.

caseStudy.scenario: A container port reports record monthly volumes for several months in succession, following a period of retail restocking and shifting trade policy. Its chief executive credits customers' choice of the port for speed, reliability and reach, while neighbouring ports compete for the same shipping lines. The port authority must decide whether to commit funds to additional handling capacity.
caseStudy.question: Critically evaluate whether the port's record volumes demonstrate a sustainable competitive advantage, and advise the port authority on how it should use these volumes in capacity and investment planning.
evidence: October's volume of about 1,026,872 TEUs was the second-highest monthly total at the port, following September's all-time record.
The port exceeded one million TEUs in consecutive months for the first time, and the article says it did so three times in the year.
From June to October the port handled nearly 5 million TEUs, its strongest five-month stretch.
The executive attributes the surge to consumer spending, inventory replenishment, trade policy changes and challenges on other global shipping routes.
plan: Define the claim and separate volume from advantage, using the resource-based view and VRIO to test whether speed, reliability and reach are valuable, rare and inimitable.
Decompose the drivers of volume into demand, replenishment, policy and diverted cargo, and note which of these the port can influence.
Apply the bullwhip effect to judge whether the peak reflects order amplification rather than sustained demand.
Apply the cost-service trade-off to test whether speed and reliability hold at high volumes, using dwell time and total logistics cost as evidence.
Assess resilience and concentration risk from reliance on one gateway and diverted cargo.

Recommend investment in controllable capacity and service measures, planning around normal volumes rather than peak months, diversifying routings, and benchmarking against rival ports before treating the volumes as proof of advantage.
pitfalls: Treating record throughput as proof of competitive advantage without evidence on service, cost or rival ports.
Misreading the records: October is the second-highest month, September holds the all-time high, and the claim that no other US port has done this is the port's own statement.

alsoConsider: Porter's five forces (rivalry among ports and shipping lines)

exam.question: Critically evaluate the view that a container port's record throughput is a reliable indicator of its competitive strength in global supply chains.
outline: Distinguish volume driven by demand and trade policy from advantage the port controls, using the resource-based view.
Assess whether throughput gains hold up on service and cost measures such as dwell time and total logistics cost, and consider bullwhip-driven peaks and concentration risk.
Conclude with the evidence needed to judge whether the advantage is sustainable, including comparisons with rival ports.

articles.title: The debate on GHG Protocol’s electricity accounting revisions is far from over
articles.takeaway: The GHG Protocol's proposed Scope 2 rules, hourly matching and same-region deliverability, look likely to survive, but the timing, the treatment of legacy power purchase agreements and the grid rules are unresolved, so companies with renewable contracts need to plan for several outcomes.
articles.summary: A late-October workshop of the GHG Protocol's technical working group, held to revise its Scope 2 electricity accounting standard, failed to settle key questions about how to transition to the new rules and how long existing renewable contracts will be recognised. The group worked through more than 1,100 consultation comments. Two proposals, hourly matching of consumption and same-region deliverability, look set to be included in the final revisions, though hourly matching may be recommended rather than required and phased in from the largest users. Legacy power purchase agreements are the main concern: the draft applies one effective date to all contracts, which the Corporate Energy Buyers Association warns could remove credit from a 15-year PPA while it is still running. Recommendations go to the independent standards board for a December meeting, final text is expected in 2027, and the Science Based Targets initiative is consulting on interim changes to its own standard.
keyPoints: Hourly matching would replace the annual calculation used for purchased electricity since 2015.
Deliverability rules would require contracts or certificates to come from the same regions where electricity is consumed.
Hourly matching may be recommended rather than mandatory and phased in over several years, starting with large consumers, with timelines discussed from 2031 to 2039.
Standardised grid boundaries would be set by the GHG Protocol or an independent authority so companies do not interpret them alone.
Incrementality flexibility would likely allow contracts where the buyer is the original offtaker, or where generation falls within an age limit of around 15 years.

modules.reading: This is a green and sustainable logistics story at its core. Scope 2 captures the emissions from purchased electricity, which warehouses, distribution centres and charging depots use heavily. The module asks how emissions are measured, reported and reduced, and this article shows that the measurement rule itself determines what a company can claim. A student should care because the choice between annual and hourly accounting, and between local and wider matching, changes reported carbon figures and therefore the credibility of any decarbonisation claim.

From a People, Work and Organisations viewpoint this is an account of externally triggered change being negotiated under pressure, where the outcome depends on who holds power and how the transition is phased. The standards board's final authority, the consultation process and CEBA's lobbying over legacy contracts show stakeholder conflict and resistance. Students should see it as a case in which the design of the transition is as contested as the goal itself.

Purchasing students will recognise power purchase agreements as long-term procurement contracts for electricity. The dispute is essentially about whether existing supply contracts keep their value under new rules. The article also touches on sustainable sourcing claims, since a buyer's green credentials depend on how its contracts are accounted for. The module would examine how contract terms, legacy agreements and buyer-supplier power affect the value of such contracts.

applications.concept: Carbon footprinting and Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions
applications.theory: Carbon footprinting measures the greenhouse gases an organisation emits, grouped into Scope 1 (direct emissions from owned sources), Scope 2 (indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat or steam) and Scope 3 (all other value-chain emissions). Scope 2 figures depend on the accounting method used to attribute electricity to emissions, so reporting rules can change a reported footprint without any change in physical operations.
applications.link: The article describes the GHG Protocol's Scope 2 standard, which governs how companies calculate and disclose emissions from purchased electricity. The proposed move from annual to hourly matching would require each hour's consumption to be matched with generation, so night-time warehouse load on a fossil-heavy grid could no longer be offset by renewable output produced at other times. The deliverability rule adds a geographic test, requiring contracts or certificates from the same regions where electricity is used. Phasing by load, starting with companies with annual loads above 10 terawatt-hours, reflects the view that large users have the data and resources to comply first.
applications.critique: The footprint is a construct of reporting conventions rather than a direct measure of physical emissions, so Scope 2 figures can be restated by rule changes alone. The article's uncertainty over legacy contracts shows how this undermines year-on-year comparability and the reliability of targets built on the old method.
applications.practice: A logistics operator should calculate Scope 2 emissions for its main sites on both the existing annual basis and an hourly basis, to see the likely restatement before it happens. It should also identify which of its electricity contracts are legacy PPAs and which would meet the proposed deliverability and incrementality conditions, and disclose its method clearly.

applications.concept: Lewin's three-step model and force field analysis
applications.theory: Lewin's model describes change in three stages: unfreezing the existing equilibrium, moving to a new state, and refreezing new behaviours so they become stable. Force field analysis identifies the driving forces pushing for change and the restraining forces resisting it, and compares their strength to judge whether change is feasible or what must be done to shift the balance.
applications.link: The driving forces are clear: the GHG Protocol's aim to tighten electricity accounting, the push for hourly matching and standardised grid boundaries, and the SBTi's need to align its target-setting with the revised standard. The restraining forces include CEBA's concern that contracts bought under the old rules could lose credit, the absence of settled dates, thresholds and readiness conditions, and the open question of how to treat legacy agreements. The proposed responses, a phased transition, recommended rather than required status and flexibility on incrementality, act as attempts to reduce restraining forces without abandoning the driving ones. Refreezing is planned only for 2027, so the new equilibrium remains provisional.
applications.critique: Lewin's model implies a sequence with a stable end state, but here the standard is an interim step with repeated consultation, so change looks more continuous than the three stages suggest. Force field analysis also tends to treat forces as fixed and measurable, whereas lobbying and data readiness shift during the process.
applications.practice: A manager at a company holding legacy contracts should list the forces for and against adopting the new rules, separating those within the company's control from those outside it. It should then target the restraining forces, for example by supporting interim contract pathways, and set a review point rather than treating the final rules as settled.

applications.concept: Externalities and carbon pricing
applications.theory: An externality is a cost or benefit of an activity that falls on third parties and is not reflected in market prices, such as the greenhouse gas emissions from electricity generation. Carbon pricing, through taxes or emissions trading, aims to internalise this cost so that polluters bear it. Accounting rules are a softer instrument: they decide how emissions are attributed and therefore which party is credited for low-carbon power.
applications.link: Emissions from electricity generation are an externality that the Scope 2 standard tries to make visible. The debate over whether a 15-year PPA keeps its credit, and whether a contract must come from the same region, is in effect a debate about who is credited with the emissions avoided by a renewable investment. The discussion of incrementality, which asks whether generation is new or the buyer is the original offtaker, reflects a concern that claimed benefits should be additional rather than relabelled from existing supply. Standardised grid boundaries stop each company drawing its own boundary around the externality.
applications.critique: Accounting attribution does not change physical emissions on the grid, so a stricter rule can improve credibility without reducing carbon in the atmosphere. Carbon pricing also internalises the cost directly, whereas disclosure relies on stakeholders acting on the information, which is a weaker incentive.
applications.practice: A logistics firm should treat the accounting debate as a signal about future carbon costs. It should model its freight and warehouse electricity exposure under a carbon price as well as under the new reporting rules, and prefer contracts that would still qualify under stricter conditions, such as those with local deliverability and new capacity.

applications.concept: Resource dependence theory (Pfeffer and Salancik)
applications.theory: Resource dependence theory holds that organisations depend on others for critical resources, and that those who control scarce or essential resources hold power over those who depend on them. Power is therefore relational, and dependence can be reduced by diversifying sources, building alternatives or forming coalitions. Organisations also try to manage the uncertainty created by their dependencies.
applications.link: The standard-setting process shows dependence running in several directions. The GHG Protocol and its independent standards board control the rulebook on which companies, the SBTi and ISO depend, and their final say gives the board considerable power. CEBA's members hold a different kind of leverage, having procured more than 50 GW of electricity, which makes their long-term contracts central to the market and gives them grounds to press for legacy treatment. The use of subgroups and the planned December recommendations show the board managing uncertainty by channelling input through defined routes, while CEBA's public statement shows buyers using an external voice to shape the outcome.
applications.critique: Resource dependence explains power through material resources but underplays legitimacy and technical expertise, which the board draws on through its process and which members can contest only through argument. It also treats dependence as static, whereas a revised standard can shift who holds the leverage.
applications.practice: Companies or industry bodies seeking a better outcome should identify what they control that the standard-setter needs, such as data, market volume or technical evidence, and offer it through formal consultation. They should build coalitions, as CEBA has done, rather than rely on individual firms, and avoid depending on a single contract route that a rule change could remove.

caseStudy.scenario: A national logistics company operates distribution centres and a growing electric delivery fleet, and holds several long-term renewable power purchase agreements, including one older 15-year contract. It reports Scope 2 emissions on an annual basis and has set a science-based target that relies on this method. A proposed revision would require hourly matching and same-region contracts, and the older contract could lose credit under a single effective date. The board must decide how to respond before the final rules are issued.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on how to respond to the proposed revisions to its Scope 2 accounting, critically evaluating the change-management and stakeholder issues involved.
evidence: Hourly matching may be recommended rather than required and phased in over several years, starting with the largest users, with timelines discussed from 2031 to 2039.
Legacy PPAs are unresolved; the current text applies one effective date to all contracts, and CEBA warns that a 15-year PPA could lose credit while it is still running.
CEBA members have procured more than 50 GW under the old rules, and the independent standards board has the final say on the revisions.
Recommendations are due to the board in early December, and final text is expected to circulate in the second quarter of 2027.
plan: Define Scope 2 and explain the proposed shift from annual to hourly matching and from wider to same-region deliverability, using the carbon footprinting framework to show how the reported emissions could be restated.
Map the forces for and against adopting the new rules using Lewin's force field analysis, and identify the restraining forces the company controls, notably its exposure through legacy PPAs.

Analyse the power of the standards board and industry bodies using resource dependence theory, showing which resources the company holds that the board needs and where the company depends on the board's decisions.
Assess the incrementality and grid boundary options against the company's contract portfolio, and evaluate how phasing by load would affect its own timeline.

Recommend a staged response: model both accounting bases, support a coalition submission on legacy contracts, set a review at the 2027 text, and communicate the remaining uncertainty in the sustainability report.
pitfalls: Treating the proposed rules as final; the article makes clear they are recommendations subject to phasing and further consultation.
Describing Lewin's model as a simple three-step sequence without identifying the specific forces, or ignoring that stakeholders can still shape the outcome.

alsoConsider: Kotter and Schlesinger's strategies for overcoming resistance to change

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether Lewin's force field analysis is adequate for managing externally imposed change in which powerful stakeholders contest both the goal and the timetable. Illustrate your answer with an example of a regulatory or standard-setting change.
outline: Define Lewin's three-step model and force field analysis, explaining driving and restraining forces with reference to the framework's purpose.
Apply the framework to a standard-setting change, identifying forces such as lobbying by contract holders, data readiness and the phasing timetable.
Critique the framework's linear and static assumptions, set out an alternative such as Kotter's model or a power-based analysis, and conclude on its usefulness.

articles.title: Autonomous Trucks Could Be Cheaper Than Human Drivers in U.S. by 2028
articles.takeaway: The autonomous-truck story is less about the technology than about who carries the cost and the change. Once driver pay falls away the economics flip, and the human side, from job security to a sense of fair process, becomes the main source of resistance.
articles.summary: The article reports Kearney and MIT Mobility Initiative research suggesting that autonomous trucking in the U.S. could match human-driven trucking on cost per mile by 2028. Autonomous costs are projected to fall from about 4 dollars a mile in 2026 while human-driven costs rise, including fuel, benefits and insurance. Europe and the Middle East are expected to reach the same point later, around 2030 and 2032, because driver costs are lower there. Goldman Sachs gives a similar 2028 estimate. Company trial figures from Bot Auto and Aurora suggest even lower costs on specific runs. The article also notes unresolved concerns: safety in bad weather and with unexpected hazards, cyber vulnerability (a U.S. Department of Transportation analysis found more than 90 threat scenarios in a remote-assistance model), and job losses for drivers. Teamsters California has sued the state over rules allowing heavy driverless trucks, arguing the risks to safety and jobs were not properly assessed.
keyPoints: Kearney and the MIT Mobility Initiative project that autonomous trucking could reach cost parity with human-driven trucking in the U.S. in 2028, with costs including fuel, employee benefits, insurance and other factors.
The projected autonomous cost falls from about 4 dollars a mile in 2026 to 3.30 in 2027 and 2.60 in 2028, while the human-driven cost rises from 2.50 to around 2.70 over the same period.

Drivers account for roughly half of a U.S. truck's cost per mile, so the U.S. has more cost to remove than regions where drivers are cheaper; the crossover is expected around 2030 in Europe and 2032 in the Middle East.
Goldman Sachs independently predicts a similar 2028 crossover.

Bot Auto reports an all-in cost of under 2 dollars a mile for a humanless commercial load, and Aurora estimates 1.84 dollars a mile on a Fort Worth to Phoenix trial. These are company estimates from trials, not independent audited costs.

modules.reading: In People, Work and Organisations this article is about how technology reshapes the world of work and the people whose jobs it changes. The driver role is being redesigned, potentially moving from operating a vehicle to supervising it remotely, and the cost forecast implies a large reduction in driver employment. The union lawsuit is a clear example of resistance to change from a stakeholder group that feels it was not properly consulted. A student should care because the forecast turns a technology question into one of job design, the psychological contract and change management.

In logistics operations the driver is typically the largest single element of the cost of road freight, so the article is about how cost per mile drives modal and operational choices. The figures given are operating costs per mile, and the article does not report service levels, utilisation, reliability or the cost of disruption. A logistics student should use the article to see why a per-mile comparison is only one input to a total cost and service decision, and why long-haul corridors such as Fort Worth to Phoenix matter for network design.

From a supply chain perspective, autonomous trucks change the economics of the road leg but also introduce new vulnerabilities. Remote assistance and connected vehicles create a cyber attack surface, and bad weather or unexpected hazards are operational disruption risks. The article shows that a cheaper transport leg does not automatically produce a more resilient chain, and that a shipper's risk exposure depends on its carriers' systems as well as its own. Students should connect this to resilience and risk management.

applications.concept: Kotter and Schlesinger's strategies for overcoming resistance to change
applications.theory: Resistance to change arises from parochial self-interest, misunderstanding, low tolerance for change and differing assessments of the situation. Kotter and Schlesinger propose a range of responses, including education and communication, participation and involvement, facilitation and support, negotiation and agreement, manipulation and co-optation, and coercion, to be chosen according to the source and strength of resistance.
applications.link: The Teamsters California lawsuit shows resistance from a group whose members stand to lose work, and its argument that regulators did not adequately assess job losses points to a perceived lack of participation and information. The projected 2028 cost crossover provides a strong economic driver that makes the change likely to proceed, so the resistance is about how and on what terms it happens rather than whether. Kearney's observation that autonomy pays off first where drivers are expensive and scarce suggests the resistance will vary by region, with different legal and labour contexts in the U.S. and Europe. The article's concerns over safety and cybersecurity are also legitimate grounds for scepticism that managers should engage with rather than dismiss.
applications.critique: Kotter and Schlesinger's strategies were developed for change within a single organisation where managers have authority over the people affected. Here the principal resisting party is an external union acting through the courts, and the change is an industry-wide, regulation-led shift, which constrains negotiation and makes coercion both unlikely and unlawful.
applications.practice: A carrier planning this change should involve drivers and their representatives early in designing remote-assistance and transition roles, and negotiate redeployment, retraining and safety commitments. It should share the evidence on safety, cost and cyber risk openly, so the workforce does not perceive the decision as one taken without them.

applications.concept: Job Characteristics Model (Hackman and Oldham)
applications.theory: The model identifies five core job characteristics, namely skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback. These shape three critical psychological states, namely experienced meaningfulness, responsibility for outcomes and knowledge of results, which in turn affect motivation, satisfaction and performance, moderated by employees' growth-need strength.
applications.link: The article describes a model in which human operators remotely assist autonomous commercial vehicles, so the driver's job would shift from physically controlling the vehicle to monitoring and supporting it from elsewhere. Over the road, autonomy and skill variety may fall as the system takes over driving, which the model predicts will reduce motivation for those who value these characteristics. Remote assistance could, however, add task significance and create a different form of feedback, depending on how the role is designed. The article focuses on cost and jobs rather than on job content, which is the gap this model helps to fill.
applications.critique: The model assumes the organisation designs the job, but here the content of the role is being set by technology, regulators and cost pressure, and the model says little about job security, which the article identifies as the central worry. It also does not address whether displaced drivers will have the skills or locations to take up remote roles.
applications.practice: Before deployment, a manager should map the current driver role against the five core characteristics, identify which are lost and which can be restored through remote assistance or monitoring roles. Those new roles should be genuinely available to existing drivers, with training and a realistic path to them, so the redesign does not simply transfer the loss to a smaller group.

applications.concept: Total logistics cost and the cost-service trade-off
applications.theory: Total logistics cost sums transport, inventory, warehousing and administration costs, and it must be assessed alongside the service level the operation delivers. Good decisions minimise total cost for a given service standard, because reducing one cost element often increases another or affects service.
applications.link: The article compares operating cost per mile, with driver costs around half of the U.S. total and fuel, benefits and insurance included, and shows the gap closing as autonomy matures. These are cost figures only, and a total logistics view would also need service measures such as delivery time, reliability and disruption. The Aurora case on the Fort Worth to Phoenix route gives an example of a long corridor where a per-mile figure is most directly relevant. Bad-weather performance and hazard handling, which the article flags as unresolved, would affect service and cost in ways the headline figures do not show.
applications.critique: Per-mile cost is a weak proxy for logistics cost when load factors, empty running, utilisation and downtime differ between human-driven and autonomous operations. The article reports none of these, and company trial figures may not reflect typical operations.
applications.practice: A logistics manager should build a total cost model lane by lane, including autonomous operating costs, service-level effects, insurance, and expected disruption costs, before deciding which lanes to pilot. The pilot should measure service and utilisation as well as cost per mile.

applications.concept: Supply chain risk management and resilience (Christopher and Peck)
applications.theory: Supply chain vulnerability depends on the chain's structure and the sources of disruption. Resilience is the capacity to reduce the likelihood and impact of disruption and to recover quickly, using measures such as visibility, flexibility, redundancy and collaboration built into the design of the network, rather than relying only on buffer stock.
applications.link: The article's point that a U.S. Department of Transportation model identified more than 90 cybersecurity threat scenarios in remote assistance shows that autonomous transport adds a digital point of failure that did not exist when a driver was in the cab. Bad weather and unexpected road hazards are operational disruption risks on the same legs. The article indicates these concerns are not yet resolved, and they would fall on shippers and carriers as well as vehicle makers. The Teamsters' lawsuit shows that regulatory and labour disruption is also a risk to the chain, and could halt or slow operations in a particular state.
applications.critique: Christopher and Peck's approach is strongest for physical supply disruption. Cyber risk needs a different kind of defence, such as security standards and monitoring, and the framework says less about regulatory and labour-related disruption, which may be the most immediate risk here.
applications.practice: A shipper should map where autonomous carriers sit within its network and identify single points of failure in the remote-assistance and software chain. It should write cybersecurity and fallback standards into contracts and keep a human-operated alternative for critical flows.

caseStudy.scenario: A U.S. freight company runs long-haul routes between Texas and Arizona and has been advised that autonomous trucks could cost less per mile than its drivers by 2028. Its drivers' union has publicly opposed the plan and is challenging related regulation in court. A trial on one corridor has reported very low per-mile costs, but the board is aware that the figures do not show service, safety or cyber risk.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on whether, when and how the company should introduce autonomous trucks, critically evaluating the cost case against the workforce, safety and cyber risks.
evidence: Kearney and the MIT Mobility Initiative project autonomous costs of about 4 dollars a mile in 2026 falling to 2.60 in 2028, while human-driven costs rise to around 2.70
Drivers account for roughly half of a U.S. truck's cost per mile, according to Kearney
A U.S. Department of Transportation analysis identified more than 90 cybersecurity threat scenarios for remote assistance of autonomous commercial vehicles
Teamsters California sued the state's Department of Motor Vehicles over rules for heavy-duty driverless trucks, arguing that risks to public safety and jobs were not adequately assessed
plan: Define the decision and identify the stakeholders, including drivers, the union, regulators, customers and shareholders, and frame the cost case as total logistics cost rather than the headline per-mile figure.
Test the cost forecast by noting that the 2028 crossover rests on projections and self-reported trial costs, and apply the cost-service trade-off to include service levels and disruption effects.
Assess the supply chain risks using Christopher and Peck's resilience framework, covering cyber, weather and hazard risks, regulatory disruption, and single points of failure.
Analyse the people impact with the Job Characteristics Model, showing which core characteristics of the driver role are lost and which a remote-assistance role might restore.
Plan the change using Kotter and Schlesinger's strategies for resistance, deciding where to involve, negotiate and communicate, and distinguishing legitimate concerns from opposition to change.
Recommend phased pilots on high-cost, driver-short lanes, with redeployment and safety commitments and agreed metrics for cost, service and safety, reviewed before any wider roll-out.
pitfalls: Treating the 2028 crossover as settled: the article presents forecasts and company trial figures, and per-mile costs leave out service levels, disruption and utilisation.
Treating drivers only as a cost line; strong answers address job design, the psychological contract and the legitimate safety and fairness concerns raised by the union.

alsoConsider: Lewin's three-step model and force field analysis

exam.question: To what extent can managers introduce automation such as autonomous trucks on cost grounds without damaging the people and organisation on which they depend? Discuss, drawing on theories of job design and organisational change.
outline: Explain how the technology changes the content of the driver's job and the psychological contract, using the Job Characteristics Model and Rousseau's psychological contract.
Assess the sources of resistance, including the legal challenge, and evaluate strategies for managing them using Kotter and Schlesinger and Lewin's force field analysis.
Conclude with a critical judgement on whether cost-led automation can be managed without addressing people, taking account of the uncertainty in the cost forecasts.

articles.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
articles.takeaway: Physical climate risk is shaping where multinationals choose to invest. Firms that avoid climate-vulnerable countries reduce one set of exposures but may give up access to growing markets and critical minerals, so location risk needs to be assessed at site level, not country level.
articles.summary: The article, by a researcher in international business, argues that multinationals increasingly treat climate vulnerability as a location risk and are steering investment away from poorer, climate-exposed countries. The author cites several studies, including his own analysis of 159 countries, finding that more climate-vulnerable countries attract less foreign direct investment. Examples include Google's abandoned Chilean data centre after a permit was revoked over water concerns, a delayed Kenyan data centre project, flood losses that reduced shareholder value at listed firms, and factory shutdowns in Thailand in 2011. The author argues that avoidance harms poor countries by reducing jobs and technology transfer, and that it also costs companies access to resources such as Congolese cobalt and Indonesian nickel, where more risk-tolerant firms have already built strong positions. He proposes three remedies: adaptation aid, climate risk insurance from development banks, and more granular local risk data.
keyPoints: Climate vulnerability is increasingly part of the location decision for factories, mines and offices, alongside traditional political and economic risks.

Several studies find that more climate-vulnerable countries receive less foreign direct investment; the author reports a 12% fall in FDI for each one-point rise on a 100-point vulnerability scale, holding other factors constant.
Companies rarely state climate reasons for avoiding a location, but visible cases include a halted US$200 million data centre in Chile and a suspended US$1 billion Kenyan project.
One analysis of 71 large listed firms found that major flood losses were followed by an average 5% fall in shareholder value over the next year, after adjusting for market movements.

Avoidance has a cost: the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world's cobalt and Indonesia is the dominant nickel producer, and more risk-tolerant firms have secured strong positions there.

modules.reading: In supply chain terms, the article is about disruption risk and the design of a sourcing and production network. Flooded factories in Thailand in 2011 halted car production at several major manufacturers, showing how a local shock can spread through a network. The concentration of cobalt and nickel supply in a few climate-exposed countries is a sourcing and supply-security problem. A student of this module should see the article as a case for building resilience into network design rather than simply exiting a region.

The article treats location as a strategic choice that shapes long-run competitive position. Environmental factors, one of the PESTEL dimensions, now carry investment-deciding weight. The author also suggests that risk-tolerant firms have built defensible positions in valuable mineral resources, which connects to resource-based arguments about advantage. Strategists should note that a cautious policy of avoidance is itself a strategic decision with consequences for access to markets and inputs.

From a finance perspective, the article describes climate risk as something that raises the cost of projects and makes them harder to finance. The 5% fall in shareholder value after major flood losses shows investors pricing physical risk. Insurance and development-bank risk sharing are presented as ways to reduce the risk premium that investors demand. A finance student should consider how climate exposure changes cash flows, discount rates and the value of risk transfer.

The article describes a mismatch in which climate damage falls mainly on countries that contributed little to emissions. Economists would see this as an externality that is not reflected in location and investment prices. The author's argument that aid for adaptation can attract investment is a claim about correcting an information or risk failure in the market. Students should note that this is a claim about correlation in the author's own study, and that causation needs more evidence.

applications.concept: Christopher and Peck: supply chain risk management and resilience
applications.theory: Supply chain risk arises from disruptions that can be internal or external to the network, and they can propagate through interconnected partners. Resilience is the capacity of a network to resist disruption and recover to an acceptable performance level. Firms reduce exposure by mapping vulnerabilities, improving visibility, and building redundancy or flexibility into sourcing and production.
applications.link: The 2011 Thai floods halted Toyota, Nissan and Honda production when local factories flooded, which shows how a single localised event can disrupt parts supply across a manufacturing network. The article's concentration of cobalt in the Democratic Republic of Congo and nickel in Indonesia represents a single-region dependency for critical inputs. Vietnam's infrastructure losses, estimated at about US$280 million for unreliable infrastructure, show how a disruption at the network's infrastructure layer can impose costs on firms. The author's point that avoidance is a blunt response maps onto Christopher and Peck's emphasis on understanding the specific vulnerabilities of each node rather than withdrawing from whole regions.
applications.critique: The framework is designed to manage risk within existing networks and says less about whether a firm should exit a country altogether, which is the decision the article is concerned with. Resilience measures such as buffer stocks or dual sourcing carry cost, and the article gives no evidence on whether they would be cheaper than the investment forgone.
applications.practice: A procurement or network director should map climate exposure at each critical site and tier, identify single-source dependencies in minerals and components, and compare the cost of dual sourcing or buffer stock against the value of access. Where exposure varies within a country, the firm should prefer site-level selection and mitigation over blanket exclusion.

applications.concept: Barney: the resource-based view and VRIO
applications.theory: A firm gains sustained competitive advantage when it controls resources that are valuable, rare, costly to imitate and organised to be exploited. VRIO is a diagnostic that tests each resource on these four dimensions. Advantage rests on resources that competitors cannot easily obtain or copy.
applications.link: The article reports that companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in the Congolese cobalt and Indonesian nickel industries. Access to these minerals is valuable and rare because the supply is concentrated in a few countries. Firms that are willing to operate in climate-exposed locations hold a capability that cautious competitors lack, which makes it difficult to imitate quickly. The author's claim that cautious firms surrender access to important resources is a VRIO argument in reverse: forgoing a valuable, rare resource means forgoing a potential source of advantage.
applications.critique: VRIO is largely static and inward-looking, and it does not explicitly account for the risk that makes a resource valuable and scarce. Climate events or expropriation could erode a resource rapidly, and the article provides no data on the returns earned by risk-tolerant firms, so the advantage claim is plausible but not demonstrated.
applications.practice: A strategy team should test whether the target resource is valuable, rare, inimitable and organised after accounting for climate exposure. If it passes, the team should consider how to secure it through local partnerships, insurance-backed projects or staged investment rather than a simple accept-or-reject decision.

applications.concept: CAPM and the weighted average cost of capital (WACC)
applications.theory: The capital asset pricing model sets the required return on equity as the risk-free rate plus beta multiplied by the market risk premium. The weighted average cost of capital blends the cost of equity and debt, and it is used as the discount rate in net present value appraisal. A higher perceived risk raises the discount rate, which lowers the present value of future cash flows and can make a project unattractive.
applications.link: The article says climate risk makes projects in vulnerable countries more expensive, less attractive and harder to finance, which corresponds to a higher discount rate or risk premium on these projects. The 5% fall in shareholder value after major flood losses at 71 listed firms suggests that investors price physical climate risk in equity values. The author's proposal that development banks provide climate insurance is effectively a means of transferring part of the cash-flow risk, which would reduce the required premium and support the project's NPV.
applications.critique: CAPM beta measures systematic market risk, but climate hazards are often location-specific and may not be captured by historic market co-movement. Applying a single country risk premium to all projects treats a city site and a rural site as equally risky, which the article itself criticises. Long horizons also make historic betas and fixed discount rates unreliable.
applications.practice: An appraisal team should model climate hazards explicitly in forecast cash flows, through lower output, higher insurance and repair costs or project delay, rather than simply raising the discount rate. They should compare project NPVs with and without available insurance and use site-specific risk assessments where possible.

applications.concept: Externalities and market failure
applications.theory: A negative externality arises when an activity imposes costs on third parties that are not reflected in market prices, leading to outcomes that are inefficient from a societal perspective. Market failure means the price system does not allocate resources efficiently. Remedies include taxes, regulation, property rights or direct provision of public goods such as adaptation infrastructure.
applications.link: Climate change is a large externality: emissions from high-income countries impose costs on low- and middle-income countries, which the article notes are responsible for only a small share of emissions yet face much of the damage. Location decisions by firms do not account for these wider welfare costs, so investment flows away from the places that most need it. The author's 2025 finding that adaptation aid is associated with more FDI fits a corrective view in which public funding reduces the perceived risk that private investors would otherwise price in.
applications.critique: Externality theory assumes that costs can be measured and internalised, but climate damage is uncertain, distributed across generations and difficult to attribute to specific investment decisions. The FDI–aid link is a correlation within the author's study and may reflect other factors, such as governance quality or existing investment ties, so causal claims should be stated cautiously.
applications.practice: A policymaker or development bank should identify the adaptation infrastructure and risk-sharing instruments that would lower the expected cost of investment in exposed regions, and should target them where the benefit to local development is greatest. A firm should treat the wider cost of avoidance, including reputational and stakeholder costs, as part of its sustainability and risk assessment.

caseStudy.scenario: A diversified mining company is considering a new cobalt processing plant in a central African country that ranks highly on climate vulnerability. Its internal risk model labels the whole country as high risk, and some competitors have already invested in neighbouring sites. Local infrastructure is fragile, and the plant would need reliable power and water supplies.
caseStudy.question: Advise the board on whether the company should invest in the proposed plant, and critically evaluate the conditions under which investment would be justified.
evidence: The author's analysis suggests a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each one-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, holding other factors constant.
Firms reporting major flood losses at 71 large listed companies saw an average 5% fall in shareholder value over the following year, after adjusting for market movements.
The Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world's cobalt, and more risk-tolerant firms have established strong positions in its mineral industry.

The World Bank already offers political risk coverage that has given companies confidence to invest in several African countries, and the author proposes climate risk insurance from development banks as a similar safety net.
plan: Define the decision using the VRIO test to establish whether access to cobalt processing is valuable, rare and difficult to imitate for this firm.
Apply the risk analysis from Christopher and Peck to map site-level exposures to flood, water, heat and power failure, and identify single points of failure in the proposed network.
Use CAPM and WACC logic to show how climate risk could raise the discount rate or reduce cash flows, and recalculate NPV for the project under base and adverse climate scenarios.

Assess the effect of insurance, development-bank risk sharing and adaptation investment on the NPV and on the risk profile, and consider whether the national risk score overstates the site-level risk.
Use the externalities argument to note the wider social and reputational consequences of exit, and weigh these against the financial case.

Recommend conditional investment: proceed only at a site that passes the local risk assessment, with insurance and adaptation measures in place, and with a defined review trigger if climate exposure changes.
pitfalls: Treating the author's 12% figure or the FDI–aid association as established causal effects rather than findings from a specific study and sample.
Assessing the investment using only the national risk score, which the article itself criticises as too coarse for site-level decisions.

alsoConsider: Kraljic's purchasing portfolio matrix, to classify critical mineral inputs by supply risk and profit impact
Dunning's eclectic (OLI) paradigm, to explain location choice for foreign direct investment
Elkington's triple bottom line, to assess social and environmental consequences alongside financial return

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether a multinational's decision to avoid investing in climate-vulnerable countries is a sound strategic response to risk, and assess the alternatives available to the firm.
outline: Define climate vulnerability as a location risk and explain how it affects investment appraisal, using evidence such as the reported FDI reduction and the shareholder value effect.
Assess the strategic costs of avoidance, drawing on resource-based arguments about access to cobalt and nickel and the growth opportunities in these markets.
Evaluate alternative responses, including site-level selection, insurance, development-bank risk sharing and adaptation aid, and recommend a course of action with clear limitations.

articles.title: Which ESG disclosures link words to action?
articles.takeaway: Not all ESG narratives are equally informative. Emphasis on sustainable value chains and renewable energy tracked better environmental performance, while frequent talk about greenhouse-gas emissions and electric vehicles showed no significant link. Judge ESG reports by which topics they stress and whether those topics connect to measurable outcomes, not by their volume.
articles.summary: Savin, López Carel and Schlindwein analysed 1,477 ESG reports from STOXX Europe 600 companies (2010 to 2023), using computational linguistics to identify the environmental themes firms emphasise. They tested these themes against independently measured KPIs such as emissions, energy use and environmental innovation. Only some themes, notably sustainable value chains and renewable energy, were consistently linked to stronger environmental performance. The author argues that the question should shift from whether ESG reports can be trusted as a whole to which parts of them carry real information, and that absence of a measurable link should not be read automatically as greenwashing.
keyPoints: Greater emphasis on sustainable value chains and on renewable energy was associated with better environmental outcomes.
Frequent discussion of greenhouse-gas emissions and electric vehicles showed no statistically significant relationship with environmental performance.
Across 34 topics, governance received the most attention, and environmental topics made up almost one-fifth of report content.
Discussion of emissions, electric vehicles, renewable energy and environmental subsidies rose over time.
The author suggests topics tied to operational decisions produce measurable outcomes sooner, while emissions strategies may take longer or be poorly captured by current indicators.

modules.reading: The article is about sustainability reporting, a core concern of supply chain sustainability. Its strongest finding concerns sustainable value chains and renewable energy, which are supply-side, operational decisions with measurable effects. A supply chain student should see this as evidence that the environmental impact of a firm lies largely in how its chain is designed and run, and that reporting on those areas is more informative than generic commitments. It also shows why sustainability must be measured across more than one dimension.

For a finance student the article concerns how investors and rating agencies read non-financial information. The author argues that counting disclosures or relying on aggregate ESG scores is inadequate, and that investors need to distinguish topics by their informational value. This connects to information asymmetry between managers and capital providers, and to the reliability of disclosure as a basis for valuation and risk assessment. Students should consider how ESG signals enter cost of capital and risk judgements.

The article examines the gap between what companies say about environmental priorities and what they achieve. In strategic planning terms, ESG reports are statements of intended strategy, while KPIs approximate realised strategy. The finding that some stated priorities track outcomes and others do not invites analysis of where intentions and results diverge, and why. Students should consider whether reporting is a communication exercise or a tool for demonstrating how priorities translate into action.

applications.concept: Triple bottom line (Elkington)
applications.theory: The triple bottom line holds that organisational performance should be assessed across economic, social and environmental dimensions together, sometimes called people, planet and profit. Each dimension should be measured and reported so that trade-offs are visible. It is widely used to frame sustainability reporting and supply chain responsibility.
applications.link: The article's strongest result concerns sustainable value chains, which relate to the environmental and supply-side dimension of the triple bottom line and are tied to operational decisions. Renewable energy deployment also produced measurable outcomes linked to environmental performance. By contrast, emissions and electric vehicle narratives, although frequently discussed, showed no significant link with the KPIs used. This suggests the environmental dimension is not uniformly reported, and that breadth of coverage across the triple bottom line does not guarantee that each dimension reflects performance.
applications.critique: The triple bottom line is a framing device rather than a measurement method, and it does not say how to weight the three dimensions when they conflict. Its breadth may encourage firms to report widely without showing which environmental claims are substantive, which is the problem the article identifies.
applications.practice: A supply chain manager applying this framework should report environmental performance using measurable indicators tied to specific operational levers, such as supplier sustainability, energy sourcing and logistics emissions. Disclosures on each dimension should be linked to the KPIs they claim to influence, with trade-offs stated explicitly.

applications.concept: Deliberate and emergent strategy (Mintzberg)
