applications.concept: Service profit chain (Heskett, Sasser and Schlesinger)
applications.link: The service profit chain proposes that employee satisfaction and retention feed into service quality, customer satisfaction and profitability. This study shows one early link in the chain: how workers perceive their scheduling affects whether they stay, which in service operations bears on continuity and the quality of delivery. The abstract does not measure service outcomes, so the wider chain is an interpretation rather than a finding of this study.
applications.practice: An operations manager in a restaurant or similar service business could treat workforce scheduling as part of service capacity planning, recognising that turnover disrupts staffing and service consistency. The student could use the service profit chain to show why scheduling decisions have operational consequences beyond HR, while noting that the article itself covers only the employee-retention step.

exam.question: Critically evaluate whether organisations should use preferential working arrangements, such as better schedules, to reward their highest-performing employees.
outline: Explain how equity theory and the psychological contract predict that employees compare their treatment with that of colleagues and respond to perceived unfairness.
Assess the potential benefits of differential rewards in motivating and retaining top performers, and the risks of turnover among the wider workforce, drawing on the restaurant study.
Recommend how managers can design and communicate reward systems that minimise perceived inequity, and identify the limits of the evidence given the study's sector and abstract-level detail.

articles.title: The Hidden Costs of Delegating to AI
articles.takeaway: Making individual tasks faster, for example by delegating them to AI, does not by itself improve overall organisational performance, because the gains depend on how the wider process and the people within it are redesigned.
articles.summary: The publisher's abstract argues that faster execution does not automatically lead to better organisational performance, and it draws its lessons from accounting firms. The title points to hidden costs of delegating work to AI, but the abstract does not say what those costs are. Only the short abstract was available, so the specific findings, figures and examples of the full piece are not known here and should be checked in the original article before being cited.
keyPoints: The abstract's central claim is that speeding up execution does not automatically improve organisational performance.
The evidence comes from accounting firms, where work is structured, checked and billed, so the lessons may transfer to other professional service settings.
The title suggests the costs lie in what delegating work to AI brings with it, but the abstract does not specify them.
The full article is needed to confirm the mechanisms and evidence before relying on them in an assignment.

applications.concept: Theory of constraints (Goldratt)
applications.link: The abstract's claim that faster execution does not improve performance fits the theory of constraints, which holds that throughput is set by the slowest step in a process. If a firm speeds up one task but review, approval or client handling remains the bottleneck, the overall output does not rise and work simply queues at the constraint. The accounting-firm lessons may show this pattern in practice.
applications.practice: A manager should map the end-to-end process and time each stage before automating anything. Automation should be targeted at the binding constraint, and success should be measured by throughput, lead time and error rates rather than the time taken for one task.

applications.concept: Job characteristics model (Hackman and Oldham)
applications.link: If delegating tasks to AI changes which work people do, it may alter skill variety, task identity, autonomy and feedback. These changes affect motivation and quality, which could offset the speed gain. The abstract's point that faster work does not automatically mean better performance suggests that people's roles need to be examined alongside the technology.
applications.practice: Before rolling out delegation, a manager could redesign roles using the five core job dimensions and check whether reviewers still have the expertise and motivation to catch errors. The student could use this model as a lens in an assignment to test the article's claims against evidence on job design.

applications.concept: VRIO framework (Barney)
applications.link: Faster execution is valuable, but if competitors can buy the same AI tools, speed is unlikely to be rare or hard to imitate. The abstract's message that speed alone does not improve performance is consistent with the view that such capabilities provide parity rather than sustained competitive advantage.
applications.practice: A strategy team could apply VRIO to the proposed AI capability and ask whether it is rare, inimitable and organised to capture value. If it fails those tests, the firm should look for complementary capabilities, such as client insight or quality assurance, that make the speed gain worth something.

exam.question: To what extent does faster task execution, such as the use of AI, improve organisational performance? Discuss with reference to process design and the management of bottlenecks.
outline: Explain how the theory of constraints shows that throughput depends on the slowest step, so speeding up one task may not raise overall output.
Assess the role of review, quality control and human judgement in automated processes, and the risk that errors or hidden work increase downstream.
Evaluate the measures of performance that should be used, such as throughput, quality, cost and customer outcomes, and conclude on when speed does and does not translate into better results.

articles.title: The HBR Guide to Killing Projects
articles.takeaway: Stopping a struggling initiative is a deliberate management decision that needs agreed criteria, not just persistence.
articles.summary: The publisher's abstract says this is a collection of seven Harvard Business Review articles. It states that the articles explain how to recognise when an initiative is not working. It also says they cover when it is time to move on from that initiative. The abstract gives no further findings, examples or recommendations, so the detail of the guide cannot be judged from this text alone.
keyPoints: The guide is a collection of seven separate HBR articles rather than a single piece of research.
Its central focus is recognising when an initiative is failing.
It also addresses the harder judgement of when to stop and move on.
The abstract gives no specific findings, so the advice itself cannot be verified from this source.

applications.concept: Escalation of commitment (Staw) and stage-gate governance
applications.link: The abstract's concern with recognising a failing initiative and knowing when to move on describes the problem that escalation of commitment creates. Teams often keep investing in a project because of earlier spending and public commitment. Stage gates with defined go or stop criteria are one way to force that review at set points.
applications.practice: A project sponsor should agree explicit kill criteria at the start, covering scope, cost, schedule and expected benefits, with a review at each gate. The student could use this abstract as a starting point for a critique of why projects continue beyond the point of recovery, and then test the suggested criteria against a named case.

applications.concept: Sunk cost principle in investment appraisal
applications.link: Deciding whether to continue or abandon an initiative is essentially an investment decision. The sunk cost principle says money already spent should not influence that choice, so only future cash flows and the value of options still open matter. The abstract's question of when to move on fits this forward-looking framing.
applications.practice: Before deciding whether to continue, a finance manager should estimate the incremental NPV of the remaining spend against the remaining benefits, ignoring costs already incurred. The student could use this to explain, in an assignment, why a project that looks costly to abandon may still be worth stopping.

exam.question: Why do organisations often persist with failing projects, and how can governance and decision criteria help them decide when to stop?
outline: Explain escalation of commitment and the psychological and political reasons projects continue despite poor progress.
Evaluate governance tools such as stage gates, independent reviews and predefined kill criteria.
Discuss how forward-looking appraisal, ignoring sunk costs, supports a sound decision to terminate a project.
